sql1.summary: Distinguish data from information, understand databases and database management systems, and see why SQL is the common language of the data industry.

slides.title: Welcome to the SQL course
slides.body:
In this 40 step, you will build the database for **Hạt**, a café with a menu, regular customers, orders and branches. You'll go from a handwritten notebook to a reporting system that uses **advanced queries**: recursive CTE, window functions, query plans, JSON and full-text search.

Each step follows the same sequence: **introduction → illustration → research → brainstorming → core concepts → applying it to Hạt → quiz**. To pass a step, your final quiz score must be at least **60%**.

slides.title: Course map
slides.body: The eight branches are eight stages. The first four are about **reading** data; the last four are about **designing, writing and optimizing** it. Return to this map whenever you feel lost.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
- How **data** differs from **information**.
- What a **database** and a **database management system (DBMS)** are.
- Why SQL, a language born in the 1970s, is still the most in-demand skill in the data industry.

No setup needed yet. From step 3 onward, you'll run SQL live in the browser right away.

slides.title: The café's notebook
slides.body: On the left is how the café recorded orders when it first opened: each line in a different style, and some lines missing a customer name. On the right is **the same data** arranged as a table: each column holds one type of information, and each row is one order. Unknown values are written as **NULL**, not left blank at random.

slides.title: Before computers: the library card cabinet

image.alt: A wooden cabinet with many small drawers holding a library's catalog cards
image.caption: Library card catalog: one card per book, ordered by author name. Photo: Grings1, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

slides.body: Libraries were already "indexing" before computers existed. Each card recorded the same fields (title, author, year, shelf location) and was sorted in a set order for fast lookup. The tables and **indexes** in SQL (stage 7) are exactly this idea, running on a machine.

slides.title: Where the real data lives

image.alt: A laptop hard drive with the cover removed, showing the magnetic platters and read head
image.caption: Hard drive with the cover off: the platters spin and the head moves. Photo: Evan-Amos, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.body: In the end, every table becomes bytes on disk (a hard drive or SSD). Reading a disk is thousands of times slower than reading RAM, so a DBMS works hard to **read the right place, as few times as possible**. That is why the 7 stage exists.

slides.title: And at scale

image.alt: Rows of server cabinets in a data center, with indicator lights and network cables
image.caption: Wikimedia Foundation server cabinets, where the Wikipedia databases are stored. Photo: Victorgrigas, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.body: Wikipedia, banks and e-commerce sites all run on racks of machines like these, and nearly all of them talk to their data using **SQL**. The SELECT query you write in step 4 runs in cabinets just like these.

slides.title: Who does what
slides.body: You (or an app) send a SQL query that says **what you need**. The DBMS decides **how to get it**: which files to read, which index to use, and in what order. Separating these two concerns is the biggest invention of the relational model.

slides.title: Data, information, knowledge
slides.body:
Information systems courses often use the **DIKW pyramid** (Ackoff, 1989):

- **Data**: raw facts, such as "8:05, peach tea, 1".
- **Information**: organized data with context, such as "today we sold 42 cups of peach tea".
- **Knowledge**: understanding drawn from information, such as "peach tea sells best in the morning, so prepare it in advance".

SQL is the tool that turns data into information.

> Ackoff, R.L. (1989) 'From data to wisdom', *Journal of Applied Systems Analysis*, 16, pp. 3–9.

slides.title: Codd's relational model (1970)
slides.body:
In 1970, Edgar F. Codd (IBM) proposed storing data as **relations**, which we call tables, and querying them with mathematical logic, **without needing to know where the data sits on disk**.

Before that, programmers had to follow pointers from one record to the next, and changing the storage meant rewriting the program. Codd called this new property **data independence**. He received the Turing Award for this work in 1981.

> Codd, E.F. (1970) 'A relational model of data for large shared data banks', *Communications of the ACM*, 13(6), pp. 377–387. doi:10.1145/362384.362685

slides.title: How SQL came about
slides.body:
Building on Codd's ideas, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce (IBM) designed **SEQUEL** in 1974, a language that reads almost like English. The name was later shortened to **SQL**.

- 1986: SQL became the ANSI standard, and 1987 became the ISO standard.
- The standard is still updated (SQL:2016 added JSON, and SQL:2023 added graph types).
- Each DBMS (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL…) follows the standard to a different degree and adds its own "dialect".

> Chamberlin, D.D. and Boyce, R.F. (1974) 'SEQUEL: A structured English query language', *Proceedings of the 1974 ACM SIGFIDET Workshop*, pp. 249–264.

slides.title: Why this course uses SQLite
slides.body:
- **Public domain**: the source code and all documentation of SQLite are in the public domain, so you can use, copy and teach it without copyright concerns.
- **Most widely deployed in the world**: built into every Android phone, iPhone, browser and a great deal of software.
- **No server needed**: the whole database is a single file, and it runs right in the browser.
- **Deep enough**: it has CTE, window functions, JSON and FTS5, which covers every advanced topic in this course.

Stage 8 shows how to carry what you've learned over to PostgreSQL and MySQL.

> SQLite (2025) *Most Widely Deployed SQL Database Engine*. Available at: https://sqlite.org/mostdeployed.html

slides.title: What does the Hạt café need to know
slides.body:
The owner of the Hạt café asks you five questions:

1. How much money did we take in today?
2. Which item sold best this week?
3. Which customer comes back most often?
4. Which hour is busiest?
5. Is this month up or down compared to last month?

With a notebook, this takes an entire evening. With a database, each question is **one SQL query** that runs in under a second. By the end of the course, you can answer all five. The 5 question needs a window function from stage 6.

slides.title: Breaking it down: what does the café track?
slides.body:
Each "thing" the café needs to track becomes a table:

- **Items** (menu_items): name, price, category.
- **Customers** (customers): name, phone number, sign-up date.
- **Orders** (orders): when, which customer, which branch.
- **Order lines** (order_items): which order, which item, how many cups.

Why split "orders" and "order lines"? One order can contain several items. The full answer is in stage 4 (normalization).

slides.title: What is a database?
slides.body:
**Database** is an **organized, interrelated** collection of data, stored so that many people and programs can use it over the long term.

Three key words:

- **Organized**: follows a predefined structure (tables, columns).
- **Interrelated**: orders point to customers and to dishes.
- **Shared**: the cashier, the owner, and the delivery app all read from one source.

slides.title: What a DBMS does
slides.body:
A **database management system** (DBMS) is the software between you and the data files. It handles:

1. **Storage**: arranges bytes on disk.
2. **Querying**: understands the SQL statement and finds the fastest way to run it.
3. **Integrity**: blocks bad data (a negative price, an order pointing to a customer who doesn't exist).
4. **Concurrency**: two cashiers clicking at the same moment still don't lose an order.
5. **Recovery**: if the power cuts mid-operation, the data stays consistent.

Spreadsheets (Excel) handle 1 well, and only part of 2.

slides.title: SQL is a declarative language
slides.body:
Imperative languages (JavaScript, Python) describe **step by step**: open the file, loop through each line, if the price is above 30000, keep it…

SQL is a **declarative** language: you describe **the result you want**.

~~~sql
SELECT name, price
FROM menu_items
WHERE price > 30000;
~~~

Read it like a sentence: *select the name and price from the menu table where the price is above 30 thousand*. You write no loop; the DBMS decides how to search.

slides.title: Four groups of SQL statements
slides.body:
| Group | Abbrev. | Example | Taught in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Query | DQL | SELECT | stages 1–3, 6 |
| Definition | DDL | CREATE, ALTER, DROP | stage 4 |
| Manipulation | DML | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE | stage 5 |
| Transaction | TCL | BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK | stage 5 |

Data people use DQL the most, which is why the course starts with SELECT.

slides.title: SQL and NoSQL
slides.body:
You'll hear about **NoSQL** (MongoDB, Redis…). These suit data without a fixed structure, or cases that need extreme speed for one access pattern.

But when the data is **related** (order → customer → dish) and must be **exactly correct** (money, inventory), relational databases remain the default. Even many large NoSQL systems have added a query language similar to SQL.

Learn SQL first, and you'll understand both worlds.

slides.title: Practice: record Hạt's orders by hand SQL
slides.body:
Open the `hat/notes.sql` file (a plain text file) and copy the 5 orders below into a table, one order per row, with the columns `giờ | món | số lượng | khách`:

1. 7h50 Lan orders 2 bạc xỉu
2. 8h02 one peach tea, walk-in customer
3. 8h10 Minh 1 black coffee, 1 bread
4. 8h15 Lan comes back and adds 1 peach tea
5. 8h30 3 bạc xỉu to go

Order 3 has two items: how do you arrange it? Write down how you chose. Stage 4 will give the standard answer.

slides.title: Self-check
slides.body:
Your table is sound if:

- Each column holds only **one kind** of information (the time column doesn't mix in customer names).
- Each cell holds only **one value** (don't write “1 coffee + 1 bread” in one cell).
- Walk-in customers are marked **NULL**, not “none” in one row and “—” in another.

These three rules are exactly **normal form 1 (1NF)**. You've just normalized data without yet knowing its name.

o: Today sold 42 cups of peach tea
quiz.why: Information is data that has been organized and given context. Here, it is the summary for one day.

Let two cashiers write at the same time
quiz.why: Integrity, recovery and concurrency are the three core tasks of a DBMS.

Programs do not depend on how data is stored on disk

sql1.title: 1. Data around us: from paper ledgers to databases

sql2.summary: Learn the vocabulary of the relational model — relation, tuple, attribute, domain, key — and read the first schema of the Hạt café.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
Step 1 shows you **why** a database is needed. This step gives you **vocabulary** to talk about it precisely:

- **Relation** (table), **tuple** (row), **attribute** (column), **domain** (set of valid values).
- **Primary key** and **foreign key** — the threads linking tables.
- **Schema** — the blueprint of the whole database.

By the end of the step, you can read the four-table schema of the Hạt café.

slides.title: Anatomy of a table
slides.body: The `menu_items` table has three **attributes** (id, name, price) and three **tuples**. The bold frame is one tuple — one item. The dashed frame is one attribute — every value in it shares the same **domain** (positive integers). The `id` column is the **primary key**: no two items share an id.

slides.title: Vocabulary of two worlds
slides.body:
| Theory (Codd) | Practice (SQL) | Spreadsheet |
|---|---|---|
| Relation | Table | Worksheet |
| Tuple | Row | Row |
| Attribute | Column | Column |
| Domain | Type + constraints | Cell format |
| Schema | CREATE TABLE | — |

Academic texts use the left column, programmers use the middle column. You need to read both.

slides.title: Mind map: the relational model
slides.body: Five concepts, two layers: **structure** (tables, columns, rows) and **constraints** (keys, domains). Most real-world data errors come from neglecting the second layer.

slides.title: Foreign keys connect the tables
slides.body: Each row of `order_items` stores `item_id` = 2. This number **points to** the row where `id = 2` appears in `menu_items`, the Peach Tea item. That is a **foreign key**. Thanks to it, the item's price and name are stored in only one place.

slides.title: A relation is a set
slides.body:
In mathematics, a **relation** is a subset of the Cartesian product of its domains:

R ⊆ D₁ × D₂ × … × Dₙ

Because a relation is a **set**, Codd derived two properties:

1. **No two tuples are identical**, so a key is needed to tell them apart.
2. **Tuples have no order**. If you want an order, you must state it explicitly with ORDER BY (step 10).

These two properties explain many of the “surprises” newcomers run into when using SQL.

> Codd, E.F. (1970) 'A relational model of data for large shared data banks', *Communications of the ACM*, 13(6), pp. 377–387.

slides.title: SQL is not fully “relational”
slides.body:
C.J. Date, the author of the most widely used database textbook, points out several places where SQL departs from theory:

- A SQL table **allows duplicate rows** if no key is declared.
- SQL has **NULL**, which makes the logic three-valued (true / false / unknown), step 9.
- Column order in SQL is meaningful (SELECT *), whereas in theory it is not.

Knowing these deviations helps you avoid bugs that the DBMS won't report.

> Date, C.J. (2015) *SQL and Relational Theory*. 3rd edn. Sebastopol: O'Reilly.

slides.title: Codd's twelve rules
slides.body:
In 1985, Codd published 12 rules to test whether a DBMS is truly “relational”. Three of these rules you will meet right away in this course:

- **Information rule**: all data is represented by values in tables.
- **Guaranteed access rule**: every value can be reached by *table name + primary key + column name*.
- **Systematic treatment of NULL**: NULL is distinct from 0 and from an empty string.

No DBMS fully satisfies all 12 rules, including SQLite and PostgreSQL.

> Codd, E.F. (1985) 'Is your DBMS really relational?', *Computerworld*, 14 October.

slides.title: Choosing a key for items
slides.body:
To tell items apart, which column should be the key?

- **Item name?** The shop may rename “Bạc xỉu” to “Bạc xỉu đá”, and every old order that points by name will break.
- **Price?** Two items sharing a price is common.
- **An auto-incrementing id**: carries no meaning and never changes.

A key with no meaning is called a **surrogate key**. A key taken from real data (an ID card number, a product code) is called a **natural key**. Hạt uses surrogate keys for every table.

slides.title: Drawing relationships among the four tables
slides.body:
Answer in words before drawing:

- A **customer** can have **many orders**; an order belongs to **at most one** customer (or a walk-in guest).
- An **order** has **many order lines**; each line belongs to **exactly one** order.
- An **item** appears in **many order lines**; each line refers to only one item.

“One-to-many” appears three times. Each time, the “many” side holds a foreign key pointing to the “one” side.

slides.title: Primary key
slides.body:
A **primary key** is one or more columns whose values are:

- **Unique**: no two rows match.
- **Never NULL**: every row has one.
- **Stable**: it does not change over time.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE menu_items (
  id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  price INTEGER NOT NULL
);
~~~

In SQLite, `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` auto-increments when you don't write an id.

slides.title: Foreign key
slides.body:
A **foreign key** is a column whose value must **actually exist** in the primary key of another table.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  item_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES menu_items(id),
  qty      INTEGER NOT NULL
);
~~~

Inserting `item_id = 99` when there is no item 99 makes the DBMS reject it. This is called **referential integrity**.

Note: SQLite only checks foreign keys when `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` is turned on. In this course it is always on.

slides.title: Candidate keys and composite keys
slides.body:
- **Candidate key**: any set of columns sufficient to tell rows apart. A customer table can have two: `id` and `phone`. Choose one as the primary key and declare the other `UNIQUE`.
- **Composite key**: a key made of several columns. In `order_items`, the pair `(order_id, item_id)` is unique, so the same order cannot list one item on two lines.

~~~sql
PRIMARY KEY (order_id, item_id)
~~~

slides.title: Domains and data types
slides.body:
A **domain** is the set of valid values for a column. SQL expresses a domain with a **type** + **constraints**:

~~~sql
price INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price > 0)
~~~

- Type `INTEGER`: integers only.
- `NOT NULL`: required.
- `CHECK (price > 0)`: no item may have a price below or equal to 0.

Store money as **whole đồng** (29000), not as floating-point numbers. Floats round incorrectly (step 5).

slides.title: Hạt café schema (draft)
slides.body: Four tables, three foreign keys. This is a draft. Stage 4 will add branches, a menu category list, and normalization to reach 3NF. Arrows go from a foreign key to the primary key it points to.

slides.title: Practice: reading the schema
slides.body:
Look at the schema on the previous slide and answer (write them in `hat/schema-draft.sql` as `-- ` comments):

1. Which table has a composite key?
2. To find which customer placed order number 7, which columns do you go through?
3. To find which items order number 7 contains and their prices, which tables do you go through?
4. Why is `orders.customer_id` allowed to NULL while `order_items.item_id` is not?

slides.title: Suggested answers
slides.body:
1. `order_items` is the `(order_id, item_id)` key.
2. `orders.id = 7` → read `orders.customer_id` → `customers.id`.
3. `order_items` (filter `order_id = 7`) → `item_id` → `menu_items` gets the name and price. You will write exactly this path using **JOIN** in step 14.
4. A walk-in guest has no account, but an order line **must always** be a real item.

quiz.q: Match the theory terms with the SQL terms.
quiz.why: Codd used mathematical terms; SQL uses everyday words.

quiz.q: Which property is NOT required of a primary key?
quiz.why: A surrogate key (auto-increment id) carries no meaning, yet it is still the best primary key.

quiz.q: Because a relation is a set, the tuples in a table have a fixed order.
quiz.why: A set has no order; to get order you must use ORDER BY.

quiz.q: Insert order_items.item_id = 99 when there is no item 99 and foreign_keys is on. Result?
o: The insert succeeds and item 99 is created automatically
The DBMS rejects it because it violates referential integrity
The insert succeeds but item_id becomes NULL
quiz.why: A foreign key forces its value to actually exist in the referenced table.

quiz.q: Fill in the keyword to declare a foreign key.
quiz.why: REFERENCES table(column) declares the foreign key right on the column.

quiz.q: Why not use the dish name as the primary key?
o: Names can change, and every old order that points to a name will break
SQL rules out a text-type key
quiz.why: A key must be stable; a name is business data and can change.

quiz.q: Which columns are foreign keys in the Hạt schema?
quiz.why: Three foreign keys: order → customer, line item → order, line item → menu item.

quiz.q: The menu_items table has ids 1, 2, 3. How many rows can the following statement add?
quiz.why: id = 2 already exists; a primary key must be unique.

quiz.q: What type should the price 29.000 be stored as?
quiz.why: Store money as integers in the smallest unit so floating-point rounding can't cause errors.

quiz.q: Which line allows a menu item to have a negative price?
quiz.why: The CHECK (price > 0) constraint is missing — NOT NULL only blocks empty cells, not negative numbers.

sql2.title: 2. Relational model: tables, rows, columns and keys

sql3.summary: Run the first SQL statement on the real database of the Hạt shop, read the result table and read the error message.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
From this step on, every lesson has a **live SQL box**: a SQLite database that sits right in your browser, preloaded with the Hạt shop's data.

- Type the statement → click **Run** (or Ctrl/⌘ + Enter).
- Edit and delete freely: reopening the slide restores the data to its original state.
- Nothing is sent to a server — everything runs entirely on your machine.

slides.title: Four tables are waiting for you
slides.body: The sample data has 4 customers, 6 menu items and 8 orders from the first three days of 10. The schema matches the draft in step 2.

slides.title: Where SQLite runs
slides.body: A DBMS usually runs on a server. Here, SQLite is compiled to **WebAssembly** and runs right in a browser tab — the same source code as SQLite on your phone.

slides.title: Why learn by running real code
slides.body:
Research on learning to program shows learners progress faster when they **try – get immediate feedback – fix** rather than just reading. Immediate feedback (a result or an error message) is what turns a mistake into a lesson.

> Hattie, J. and Timperley, H. (2007) 'The power of feedback', *Review of Educational Research*, 77(1), pp. 81–112.

slides.title: WebAssembly
slides.body:
WebAssembly (Wasm) is a machine-code format for browsers, recognized as a W3C standard in 2019. It lets software written in C — such as SQLite — run at near-native speed inside the browser's safe sandbox.

> W3C (2019) *WebAssembly Core Specification*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/wasm-core-1/

slides.title: The shop owner's first question
slides.body:
"What dishes does the shop sell?"

Translated into SQL: **select every column from the menu table**. This sentence has two parts — *what to select* (SELECT) and *from where* (FROM). Every query you write in this course starts with these two parts.

slides.title: Your first SQL statement
slides.body: Click **Run**. The `*` means "all columns". The `;` ends the statement.

slides.title: Reading the result table
slides.body:
The result of SELECT **is also a table**: it has column names and rows. This matters — because the result is a table, you can query it further (stages 3 and 6).

Try changing `menu_items` to `customers`. The customer **An** currently shows the phone number **NULL** — unknown, not an empty string.

slides.title: Multiple statements at once
slides.body: The SQL box can run several statements, separated by `;`. The table shown is the result of the **last statement**. Try adding `SELECT * FROM orders;` at the end.

slides.title: Uppercase or lowercase
slides.body:
SQL **is case-insensitive for keywords**: `select`, `SELECT`, `Select` are all the same. Common conventions:

- Write keywords in **UPPERCASE**: SELECT, FROM, WHERE.
- Write table and column names in **lowercase**, joined by underscores: `menu_items`, `ordered_at`.

Text data goes in **single quotes**: `'Trà đào'`. Double quotes are for column/table names with special characters.

slides.title: Reading error messages
slides.body:
The statement below is **intentionally wrong**. Click Run and read the errors:

- `no such table` — wrong table name.
- `no such column` — wrong column name.
- `syntax error` — wrong syntax, usually from a missing comma or a mistyped keyword.

An error always points to **which word** causes the problem. Fix it to `menu_items` and run again.

slides.title: Comments in SQL
slides.body:
Two kinds of comments:

~~~sql
-- chú thích một dòng
/* chú thích
   nhiều dòng */
SELECT * FROM orders; -- cũng đặt được cuối dòng
~~~

Use comments to record **why** you wrote the query this way — the next reader (even you, 3 months later) will be grateful.

slides.title: Apply it: exploring Hạt data
slides.body:
Run `SELECT *` on all four tables in turn and answer:

1. How many menu items of type `tea` does the shop have?
2. How many rows does order number 3 have in `order_items`?
3. How many orders have no customer (customer_id is NULL)?

Write your answers in `hat/first.sql` as comments.

slides.title: Answers
slides.body:
1. **2 items**: Peach tea, Matcha latte.
2. **2 rows**: black coffee and bread.
3. **2 orders**: numbers 2 and 5 — walk-in customers.

You just counted by eye. From step 12, `COUNT` and `GROUP BY` will count for you across millions of rows.

slides.title: Exercise: view every order
slides.body: Write a SQL statement that shows the **entire orders table**. Click **Run & check** — the box automatically compares your result with the requirement.

hints: The orders table is named orders.

quiz.q: What does the * in SELECT * mean?
quiz.why: SELECT * takes all columns of the table after FROM.

quiz.q: Run the following two statements — which statement does the table shown belong to?
quiz.why: The SQL box shows the result of the last statement.

quiz.q: select * from menu_items; and SELECT * FROM menu_items; give the same result.
quiz.why: The keyword SQL is case-insensitive.

quiz.q: What does the error "no such column: prise" mean?
quiz.why: The column is named price, not prise.

quiz.q: Fill in the missing keyword.
quiz.why: FROM only names the source table.

quiz.q: How do you write the text value Trà đào in SQL?
quiz.why: Strings use single quotes; double quotes are for identifiers.

quiz.q: Which comment styles are valid in SQL?
quiz.why: The SQL standard has -- and /* */.

quiz.q: The result of a SELECT statement is also a table.
quiz.why: So you can query the result further (subqueries, CTE).

sql3.title: 3. SQLite in the browser: run the first SQL statement

sql4.summary: Select exactly the columns you need, alias them, compute new columns with expressions, and drop duplicate rows with DISTINCT.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
`SELECT *` is handy for exploring, but in real applications you almost **never** use it. This step teaches:

- Choosing **the exact columns** you need.
- Giving columns **aliases** (AS) so they are easy to read.
- Computing **new columns** with expressions: discounted price, money in thousands of dong.
- **DISTINCT**: removing duplicate rows.

slides.title: Mind map: SELECT
slides.body: The six branches are six things you can place after the word SELECT or around it. By the end of the step, you can use all six.

slides.title: In what order does the DBMS read a SELECT statement?
slides.body: You **write** SELECT first, but the DBMS **runs** FROM first: it gets the table, then selects and computes the columns, then removes duplicates. Remembering this order helps you understand why "column does not exist" errors appear in steps 6 and 13.

slides.title: Why avoid SELECT *
slides.body:
The performance guides for the major DBMSs all recommend listing specific columns:

1. **Less data**: read and send only the columns you need.
2. **Covering indexes**: the DBMS can answer from an index alone without reading the table (step 35).
3. **Robustness**: adding a column to a table does not break code that reads columns by position.

> Winand, M. (2012) *SQL Performance Explained*. Vienna: Markus Winand. Available at: https://use-the-index-luke.com/

slides.title: Projection in relational algebra
slides.body:
In Codd's theory, selecting columns is the **projection** operation (symbol π):

π\_{name, price}(menu\_items)

Because a relation is a **set**, projection removes duplicate rows automatically. SQL does **not** — to remove duplicates you must write DISTINCT. This is one of the places where SQL departs from the theory that step 2 mentions.

> Elmasri, R. and Navathe, S.B. (2016) *Fundamentals of Database Systems*. 7th edn. Boston: Pearson, ch. 8.

slides.title: What the menu screen needs
slides.body:
The ordering app of Hạt shows only the **name** and **price** (in thousands of dong, e.g. "29k"). No need for an id or a category.

Two questions before writing SQL:

1. Which **columns** are needed? → name, price.
2. Is any **transformation** needed? → price / 1000.

slides.title: Selecting specific columns
slides.body: List the column names, separated by commas. The column order in the result is **the order you write them**.

slides.title: Aliases with AS
slides.body: `AS` gives a new name to a column in the result — it does not rename the column in the table. Names with spaces or Vietnamese diacritics should be wrapped in double quotes.

slides.title: Computed columns
slides.body:
After SELECT you can place an **expression**: arithmetic, functions, string concatenation.

- `+ - * /` for numbers. Note: `29000 / 1000` gives **29** because two integers divided together drop the fractional part; to get a real number, use `29000 / 1000.0`.
- `||` concatenates strings with SQLite and follows the SQL standard.

slides.title: DISTINCT: removing duplicate rows
slides.body: The menu table has 6 items but only 3 **categories**. `DISTINCT` applies to **the whole result row** — writing `DISTINCT category, price` removes duplicates by the pair, not by category alone.

slides.title: SELECT does not need FROM
slides.body: SQLite lets you SELECT expressions without a table — handy as a calculator or for trying a function before using it for real.

slides.title: Formatting a SQL statement for readability
slides.body:
Long SQL statements should be broken across lines by clause, with one column per line when there are several:

~~~sql
SELECT
  name,
  price / 1000 || 'k' AS gia
FROM menu_items;
~~~

The DBMS doesn't care about whitespace — readers do.

o: Reads unnecessary data and breaks easily when columns are added to the table
Runs but returns the wrong result

sql4.title: 4. SELECT and FROM: select columns, alias them, remove duplicates

sql5.summary: Understand the five storage classes of SQLite, how to store money and date/time correctly, casting with CAST, and the nature of NULL.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
Choosing the wrong type is a 'silent' error: the data still stores, but arithmetic, comparisons and sorting give wrong results.

- The five storage classes of SQLite.
- Storing **money** and **date/time** correctly.
- `typeof()` and `CAST`.
- **NULL** and why it 'spreads'.

When this step is done, you have finished **chapter 1**.

slides.title: Mind map: data types
slides.body: SQLite has only five storage classes. PostgreSQL and MySQL have more types (DATE, DECIMAL, BOOLEAN…), but all of them reduce to these five.

slides.title: SQLite's dynamic typing
slides.body:
Unlike most DBMSs, SQLite attaches the type to the **value**, not the column: a column declared `INTEGER` can still hold text. A column's declared type is only a **type affinity** (type affinity): SQLite tries to convert the value to that type if it can.

From 3.37 (2021) onward, a table declared `STRICT` enforces strict typing like other DBMSs. The course uses explicitly declared types and CHECK constraints to behave like PostgreSQL.

> SQLite (2025) *Datatypes In SQLite*. Available at: https://sqlite.org/datatype3.html (public domain).

slides.title: Money must never use floating-point numbers
slides.body:
Real numbers (floating-point per IEEE 754) cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Adding 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. With money, being off by one dong means the books are wrong.

There are two standard approaches: store **integers in the smallest unit** (dong, xu), which is what this course does, or use the exact **DECIMAL/NUMERIC** type in PostgreSQL.

> Goldberg, D. (1991) 'What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic', *ACM Computing Surveys*, 23(1), pp. 5–48.

slides.title: Dates and times in ISO 8601
slides.body:
The international standard ISO 8601 writes dates and times from **largest to smallest**: `2026-10-01 07:50`. Because of this, comparing strings is also comparing times, and sorting text also sorts by time.

Writing dates in the Vietnamese style `01/10/2026` in a database, "02/01/2026" < "15/12/2025" — completely wrong.

> ISO (2019) *ISO 8601-1:2019 Date and time — Representations for information interchange*. Geneva: ISO.

slides.title: What type should each column of Hạt be?
slides.body:
| Column | Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| price | INTEGER | money in dong |
| qty | INTEGER | number of cups |
| name, category | TEXT | text |
| ordered_at | TEXT (ISO 8601) | correct comparison and sorting |
| phone | TEXT | has leading 0, no arithmetic |

A phone number stored as INTEGER loses its leading 0 — a classic mistake.

slides.title: typeof(): what type is this value?
slides.body: Run it to see the actual type of each value. Note that `phone` for An is **null** — not an empty text.

slides.title: Integers and reals
slides.body: A number with a decimal point is REAL. Dividing two integers is integer division. Look at the result of `0.1 + 0.2` — that is why money must be INTEGER.

slides.title: CAST: type conversion
slides.body: `CAST(giá_trị AS kiểu)` converts types explicitly. A string that is not a number, when cast to INTEGER, becomes 0 in SQLite (in PostgreSQL, it raises an error).

slides.title: Dates and times are TEXT with rules
slides.body: SQLite has no separate DATE type, but it has the functions `date()`, `time()`, `datetime()`, `strftime()` that work on ISO 8601 strings. Stage 2 uses them to filter orders by date and by time.

slides.title: NULL means "unknown"
slides.body:
NULL is not 0, and not an empty string — it means **unknown**. Consequences:

- Any arithmetic involving NULL gives **NULL**: `NULL + 1` is NULL.
- Comparing with NULL gives **NULL**, even `NULL = NULL`.
- To check for it, use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` (step 9 covers this in depth).

slides.title: coalesce(): replace NULL with a default value
slides.body: `coalesce(a, b, …)` returns the **first value that is not NULL**. Use it for display: if a customer has no phone number, show a placeholder text.

slides.title: Exercise 1: the type of the price
slides.body: Show the item name and the **data type** of the price column (use typeof), with the alias `kieu`.

hints: The function typeof(column) returns the type name.
SELECT name, typeof(price) AS kieu FROM menu_items;

slides.title: Exercise 2: the date of each order
slides.body: Show `id` and **only the date part** of `ordered_at` for every order.

hints: The date() function extracts the date part.

slides.title: Exercise 3: a contact list with no gaps
slides.body: Show the customer name and phone number; for customers without a phone number, show `0000000000`.

slides.title: Stage 1 summary
slides.body:
You have:

1. Distinguished data from information; understood the DBMS and Codd's relational model.
2. Read a schema with primary and foreign keys.
3. Ran a real SQL, read its results and errors.
4. Wrote SELECT with columns, aliases, expressions, and DISTINCT.
5. Chose the correct types and handled NULL.

Stage 2: **WHERE** — ask the right question to get exactly the rows you need.

quiz.why: Integers in the smallest unit: no rounding errors.

quiz.why: Dividing two integers performs integer division.

quiz.why: Comparing with NULL gives NULL; you must use IS NULL.

quiz.q: Why store phone numbers as TEXT?
o: Keep the leading 0 digit(s) and don't do arithmetic on it
quiz.why: Storing as INTEGER would lose the leading 0 digit(s).

quiz.q: Fill in a function that returns the first value that is not NULL.
quiz.why: coalesce(a, b, …) returns the first value that is not NULL.

quiz.q: Which date format sorts and compares correctly when stored as text?
quiz.why: ISO 8601 writes from largest to smallest unit, so text order matches time order.

quiz.q: Cast the value to type SQLite.
quiz.why: Five storage classes: integer, real, text, blob, null.

quiz.why: Concatenating with NULL also gives NULL.

quiz.q: What is the result?
quiz.why: SQLite casts a non-numeric string to 0 (PostgreSQL will raise an error).

sql5.title: 5. Data types: numbers, text, date-time and NULL

sql6.summary: Filter exactly the rows you need with WHERE and six comparison operators, comparing numbers, text and date-times.

slides.title: Stage 2: ask the right questions
slides.body:
Stage 1, you take **every row**. In practice, shop owners always ask with conditions: a dish *over 30 thousand*, an order *this morning*, a customer *without a phone number*.

Stage 2 has 6 steps: WHERE → AND/OR/IN/BETWEEN → LIKE → NULL → ORDER BY and pagination → CASE and functions. Stage outcome: a menu page filtered by price, category and keyword.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 2
slides.body: Seven branches are the seven tools you'll have after this stage. This step covers the first branch: **comparison**.

slides.title: How WHERE works
slides.body: The DBMS goes through **each row**, evaluating the condition. TRUE keeps it, FALSE or NULL drops it. The result table keeps only the rows that pass.

slides.title: Selection in relational algebra
slides.body:
Filtering rows is the **selection** operation (symbol σ) from Codd:

σ\_{price > 30000}(menu\_items)

Note: "SELECT" of SQL is the **projection** operation (choosing columns), while the **selection** of rows is WHERE. This naming mismatch confuses many learners, so now you know.

> Elmasri, R. and Navathe, S.B. (2016) *Fundamentals of Database Systems*. 7th edn. Boston: Pearson, ch. 8.

slides.title: Translating questions into conditions
slides.body:
| Shop owner's question | Condition |
|---|---|
| Dishes over 30 thousand | `price > 30000` |
| Tea-category dishes | `category = 'tea'` |
| All dishes except food | `category <> 'food'` |
| Orders from date 2/10 | `ordered_at >= '2026-10-02'` |

Each condition is a **predicate** that evaluates to true or false for each row.

slides.title: Six comparison operators
slides.body:
| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `=` | equal |
| `<>` or `!=` | not equal |
| `<` `<=` | less than (or equal) |
| `>` `>=` | greater than (or equal) |

SQL uses **one** `=` sign for comparison (unlike JavaScript). `<>` is the SQL standard, `!=` is a dialect accepted by most DBMSs.

slides.title: Comparing text
slides.body: String comparison follows character order. By default SQLite is **case-sensitive** when used with `=`: `'Tea'` is not equal to `'tea'`. Add `COLLATE NOCASE` to ignore case (for unaccented text).

slides.title: Comparing dates and times
slides.body: Because dates and times are stored in ISO 8601 (step 5), comparing strings is in fact comparing times. `'2026-10-02'` is less than `'2026-10-02 09:00'` because the shorter string comes first.

slides.title: WHERE with expressions
slides.body: Both sides of a comparison can be expressions. For example: items whose price after a 10% discount is still above 30 thousand. Avoid wrapping the column in a function when you can. The 7 step explains why it drops the index.

slides.title: Aliases cannot be used in WHERE
slides.body: The query below is **intentionally wrong**: WHERE runs **before** SELECT (recall the step 4 diagram), so when filtering, the alias `gia_k` does not exist yet. PostgreSQL raises an error; SQLite sometimes accepts it as an extension, so don't rely on it. Repeat the expression instead.

slides.title: Exercise 1: cheap items
slides.body: Show the names and prices of items **25 thousand or less**.

slides.title: Exercise 2: not coffee
slides.body: Show the names of items whose category is **not** `coffee`.

slides.title: Exercise 3: orders dated 1/10
slides.body: Show `id` orders placed **before** the date 2/10/2026.

hints: Compare ordered_at with an ISO date string.

quiz.q: In SQL, which clause filters ROWS?
quiz.why: WHERE is the selection σ; SELECT is the projection (columns).

quiz.q: How many rows? (prices: 29k, 35k, 25k, 20k, 45k, 39k)
Fill in the "not equal" operator per the SQL standard.
quiz.why: <> is the standard; != is a common dialect.

quiz.q: WHERE category = 'Tea' finds items whose category is 'tea' in SQLite (default).
quiz.why: = is case-sensitive by default.

quiz.q: Why can't you use the alias SELECT in WHERE?
o: WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet
quiz.why: Processing order: FROM → WHERE → SELECT.

quiz.q: What is the result?
quiz.why: A shorter string is a prefix, so it comes first → TRUE (1).

quiz.q: Match each question with a condition.
quiz.why: Each question becomes one true/false condition.

quiz.q: WHERE drops the rows where the condition evaluates to what?
quiz.why: Only rows where the result is TRUE are kept.

sql6.title: 6. WHERE and comparison operators

sql7.summary: Combine multiple conditions with AND, OR, NOT; write them compactly with IN and BETWEEN; avoid operator-precedence traps.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
Real questions rarely have just one condition: "tea **or** coffee, **and** under 40 thousand". This step teaches:

- AND, OR, NOT and **operator precedence**.
- IN — writing many ORs compactly.
- BETWEEN — a range of values.

slides.title: AND truth table
slides.body: AND is TRUE only when **both** operands are TRUE. The NULL cell is explained in detail in step 9 — for now, remember: FALSE AND anything is FALSE.

slides.title: Boolean algebra
slides.body:
AND, OR, NOT are the three operations of **Boolean algebra** (George Boole, 1854). Two De Morgan laws help simplify conditions:

- NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
- NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

> Boole, G. (1854) *An Investigation of the Laws of Thought*. London: Walton and Maberly.

slides.title: Write the condition in words first
slides.body:
"Drinks in the tea or coffee category, priced under 40 thousand."

The sentence is ambiguous: does "under 40 thousand" apply to both categories or only coffee? The shop owner means **both**. Write it out with parentheses:

(category = tea OR category = coffee) AND price < 40000

SQL also needs exactly those parentheses.

slides.title: AND and OR
slides.body: AND narrows the result (every condition must hold); OR widens it (one match is enough).

slides.title: Operator-precedence trap
slides.body: **AND binds tighter than OR**. The query below has no parentheses, so it is read as `tea OR (coffee AND price < 30000)` — Matcha 45k slips in! Add parentheses around the two OR operands and run it again.

slides.title: NOT
slides.body: NOT inverts a condition. Writing `<>` or `NOT IN` is usually easier to read than putting NOT in front of the whole expression.

slides.title: IN: much more compact than many ORs
slides.body: `cột IN (a, b, c)` is equivalent to `cột = a OR cột = b OR cột = c`. `NOT IN` is the negated form — be careful when the list contains NULL (step 9).

slides.title: BETWEEN: a range of values
slides.body: `BETWEEN a AND b` **includes both endpoints**: it is equivalent to `>= a AND <= b`. With date-times, be careful: `BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-02'` **misses** orders placed on 09:00 on day 2/10 — use `>= ngày đầu AND < ngày sau` to be safe.

slides.title: Exercise 1: tea or coffee under 40k
slides.body: Show the drinks in the `tea` **or** `coffee` category that cost **under 40000**.

hints: Remember the parentheses around the two OR operands, or use IN.

slides.title: Exercise 2: Lan's and Vy's orders
slides.body: Customer Lan has id 1 and Vy has id 4. Show `id` and `ordered_at` all orders for both customers.

hints: Use IN with a list of ids.

slides.title: Exercise 3: orders on 2/10
slides.body: Show `id` all orders **on 2/10/2026** (from 00:00 up to, but not including, 00:00 on 3/10).

hints: Half-open range: >= the first day AND < the day after.

quiz.q: In SQL, which operator has higher precedence?
quiz.why: AND before OR — always add parentheses when mixing the two.

quiz.q: How many rows are there?
quiz.why: 25k, 29k, 35k — BETWEEN includes both endpoints.

quiz.q: Write it compactly: category = 'tea' OR category = 'food'
quiz.why: IN replaces a chain of ORs on the same column.

quiz.q: NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B).
quiz.why: De Morgan's law.

quiz.q: The safest way to filter orders on 2/10 is?
quiz.why: A half-open range misses no hours or minutes.

quiz.q: Which row causes Matcha 45k to appear in the result of "tea or coffee under 30k"?
quiz.why: Missing parentheses: the AND binds to the coffee branch first.

quiz.q: Which expression is equivalent to price >= 25000 AND price <= 35000?
quiz.why: BETWEEN includes both endpoints; the 3 clause is De Morgan's law.

sql7.title: 7. AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN

sql8.summary: Pattern matching on strings with LIKE and GLOB, using the string functions lower, instr, length, and understanding LIKE's limits with Vietnamese.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
A customer types "cà" in the search box — the app should show *Cà phê đen*. This step teaches:

- LIKE with `%` and `_`.
- GLOB (case-sensitive, Unix-style).
- String functions: `lower`, `instr`, `length`, `substr`.
- The limits of LIKE — why stage 7 needs FTS5.

slides.title: Wildcards
slides.body:
| Pattern | Matches | Does not match |
|---|---|---|
| `'Cà%'` | Cà phê đen | Bạc xỉu |
| `'%trà%'` | Trà đào? (depending on case) | Bánh mì |
| `'B_nh mì'` | Bánh mì | Bạc xỉu |

`%` = **0 or more** characters. `_` = **exactly 1** characters.

slides.title: LIKE in the SQL standard
slides.body:
LIKE comes from the SQL-86 standard. SQLite makes LIKE **case-insensitive only for ASCII letters** (A–Z): `'TRÀ'` and `'trà'` don't match because "À" and "à" lie outside ASCII.

A common approach: store an extra "normalized" column (lowercase, no accents) to search on — stage 4 does this with a generated column.

> SQLite (2025) *SQL Language Expressions — The LIKE, GLOB, REGEXP, MATCH operators*. Available at: https://sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#like (public domain).

slides.title: Menu search box
slides.body:
The user types `x` → the sentence SQL: `WHERE name LIKE '%' || x || '%'`.

Three issues to think about:

1. Typing with different letter case.
2. Typing without diacritics ("ca phe").
3. A table with 1 million rows: `%x%` cannot use an index → slow.

This step solves (1) with unaccented text; (2) and (3) are left for stage 4 and 7.

slides.title: LIKE with %
slides.body: Find items that **start with** "C". Try changing it to `'%a%'` (contains the letter a) and `'%h'` (ends with h).

slides.title: LIKE with _
slides.body: `_` matches exactly one character. The pattern `'_______'` (7 underscores) finds names exactly 7 characters long — Bạc xỉu, Trà đào, Bánh mì.

slides.title: Case-insensitive matching
slides.body: For ASCII text, LIKE in SQLite already ignores case. To be sure on every DBMS, normalize both sides with `lower()`.

slides.title: GLOB
slides.body: GLOB uses `*` and `?` (as on the Unix command line) and **is always case-sensitive**. It also has character classes: `[A-C]*` = starts with A, B or C.

slides.title: Commonly used string functions
slides.body: `length` counts characters, `instr(s, x)` returns the position of x in s (0 if absent), `substr(s, từ, dài)` cuts a substring, `replace` replaces, `trim` trims spaces from both ends.

slides.title: Matching a literal % or _ character
slides.body: To find an actual % character ("10% off"), declare an escape character with `ESCAPE`: `LIKE '%10\%%' ESCAPE '\'`.

slides.title: Exercise 1: items with the word "latte"
slides.body: List the items whose names contain `latte` (case-insensitive).

hints: Wrap the keyword in % on both sides.

slides.title: Exercise 2: multi-word names
slides.body: List the items **that contain a space** (names of two or more words).

hints: The pattern has one space in the middle.

slides.title: Exercise 3: phone numbers ending in 4
slides.body: List the customers whose phone number **ends in 4**.

hints: % goes first, the character to find goes last.

quiz.q: What does % in LIKE match?
quiz.why: _ is exactly 1 character; % is any string, including an empty one.

quiz.q: How many items match? (Bạc xỉu, Trà đào, Cà phê đen, Bánh mì, Matcha latte, Cold brew)
quiz.why: Bạc xỉu, Bánh mì.

quiz.q: GLOB in SQLite is case-sensitive.
quiz.why: GLOB is always case-sensitive; LIKE is not (for ASCII).

quiz.q: Fill in the pattern to find names that end in 'brew'.
quiz.why: % goes first, brew goes last.

quiz.q: Why is LIKE '%trà%' often slow on a very large table?
o: A pattern starting with % cannot use a normal index
quiz.why: It must scan every row — stage 7 uses FTS5.

quiz.q: What is the result?
quiz.why: Counting positions from 1: C-o-l-d-␠ is 5 characters, and brew starts at 6.

quiz.q: Match each pattern with its meaning.
quiz.why: % any, _ one character.

sql8.title: 8. LIKE, GLOB and string search

sql9.summary: Understand the three-valued logic of SQL, filter with IS NULL, avoid the NOT IN trap with NULL, and use IS DISTINCT FROM.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
NULL is the number one source of errors for people new to SQL — queries run fine but **return missing rows**. This step teaches:

- Three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, **UNKNOWN**.
- `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`.
- The `NOT IN` trap with NULL.
- `IS` / `IS NOT` for a "safe comparison with NULL".

slides.title: Three-valued truth table
slides.body: Read the middle cell: TRUE AND NULL = NULL (unknown), FALSE AND NULL = FALSE (certainly false). With OR it is the reverse: TRUE OR NULL = TRUE.

slides.title: The debate over NULL
slides.body:
Codd (1979) introduced NULL into the model to represent "missing information". C.J. Date strongly objected: three-valued logic makes many familiar laws no longer hold — for example `x = x` is not always TRUE.

Practical lesson: **declare NOT NULL on every column that can hold one** (stage 4), and always ask "what if this column is NULL?" when writing WHERE.

> Codd, E.F. (1979) 'Extending the database relational model to capture more meaning', *ACM TODS*, 4(4), pp. 397–434.
>
> Date, C.J. (2015) *SQL and Relational Theory*. 3rd edn. O'Reilly, ch. 4.

slides.title: The shop owner's question
slides.body:
"How many orders are **not** Lan's (id 1)?"

A quick query: `WHERE customer_id <> 1`. The result is **missing** two walk-in customer orders — because `NULL <> 1` is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

The correct answer must state it clearly: different from 1 **or** no customer at all.

slides.title: Comparing with NULL always gives NULL
slides.body: Count the rows of the query below: only 4, not 6. The two walk-in orders disappear.

slides.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
slides.body: Check NULL **only** with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. `= NULL` always gives NULL, so it never matches any row.

slides.title: IS: safe comparison with NULL
slides.body: SQLite has `IS` / `IS NOT` used like `=` / `<>` but treats two NULL as equal. The SQL standard writes `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` / `IS DISTINCT FROM` (PostgreSQL supports it).

slides.title: The NOT IN trap
slides.body: `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL` — the second part is always UNKNOWN, so **no rows** are selected. This bug often occurs when the list comes from a subquery (step 16). The query below returns 0 rows.

slides.title: NULL in display expressions
slides.body: `coalesce` (step 5) and `ifnull(a, b)` replace NULL in display. `nullif(a, b)` does the opposite: returns NULL if a = b — useful to avoid dividing by 0.

sql10.summary: Sort by one or more columns, place NULL first or last, take the top N, and paginate with OFFSET as well as keyset.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
Remember step 2: a table has **no order**. To ask for "the most expensive item", "the newest order", or "page 2 of the menu", you must state it explicitly with:

- ORDER BY (ascending/descending, multiple columns, NULLS FIRST/LAST).
- LIMIT and OFFSET.
- **Keyset** pagination, the approach large apps use.

slides.title: Position of ORDER BY and LIMIT
slides.body: ORDER BY and LIMIT run **last**, after SELECT. So ORDER BY can use column aliases, but WHERE cannot.

slides.title: OFFSET slows down over time
slides.body:
`OFFSET 100000` forces the DBMS to **read and discard** 100.000 rows before returning the 20 rows it needs. The deeper the page, the slower it gets, and if rows are inserted during paging, users see duplicates or miss rows.

**Keyset** pagination (the "seek method") remembers the last value of the previous page and filters on `WHERE id < giá_trị_cuối`, which is just as fast on every page.

> Winand, M. (2013) *We need tool support for keyset pagination*. Available at: https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset

slides.title: The app's menu page
slides.body:
- Default: **cheapest items first**; for the same price, sort by **name**.
- Each page shows 2 items (small sample data; real data would be 20).
- A "Load more" button at the bottom.

Question: what if items with the same price aren't sorted by name? → The order among items with the same price is **undefined**, so paging may repeat items. Always end ORDER BY with a unique "tiebreaker" column.

slides.title: ORDER BY ascending and descending
slides.body: `ASC` (default) ascending, `DESC` descending. Try switching to `DESC`.

slides.title: Sort by multiple columns
slides.body: Sort by the first column; ties are broken by later columns. Each column has its own direction.

slides.title: Where NULL goes
slides.body: SQLite (and MySQL) treat NULL as **smallest**: first when ASC. PostgreSQL is the opposite. Write `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` explicitly so every DBMS gives the same result.

slides.title: LIMIT: top N
slides.body: 3 most expensive items. LIMIT **without ORDER BY** takes 3 arbitrary rows, which is almost always a bug.

slides.title: OFFSET: page n
slides.body: Page n (counting from 1), k rows per page: `LIMIT k OFFSET (n - 1) * k`. This is page 2, with 2 items per page.

slides.title: Keyset pagination
slides.body: The previous page ends at the item priced 29000, id 1. The next page takes items **after the pair (29000, 1)**. Compare the set of values `(a, b) > (x, y)` from SQLite 3.15.

slides.body: Show `category`, `name`: sort by category A→Z; within the same category, by name A→Z.

slides.body: Show `name`, `price` of the cheapest dishes **ranked 2 and 3**.

o: The DBMS must read and then discard every row before it

sql11.summary: Classify data with CASE, compute dates and times with date/strftime, round and format numbers — then combine everything into a complete menu page query.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
The final step of stage 2: turn raw data into something users can read.

- **CASE**: classify as "cheap / mid-priced / expensive".
- **Date and time**: weekday, hour, adding and subtracting days.
- **Numbers**: round, abs, printf to format money.
- Stage project: a menu page query with filter + sort + pagination.

slides.title: CASE goes branch by branch
slides.body: CASE checks the WHEN clauses **from top to bottom** and stops at the first condition that is true. If no WHEN is true, it returns the ELSE value; if there is no ELSE, the result is NULL.

slides.title: CASE — the conditional expression of SQL
slides.body:
CASE has existed since SQL-92 and is the **standard** way to write conditions inside an expression (instead of each DBMS's own IF/IIF). Because it is an expression, CASE can go in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, and even inside aggregate functions (step 12 uses it for conditional counting).

> ISO/IEC (1992) *ISO/IEC 9075:1992 Database Language SQL*, §6.9 <case expression>.

slides.title: Price labels on the menu
slides.body:
The shop owner wants every dish to have a label:

- under 30 thousand → **cheap**
- under 40 thousand → **mid-priced**
- otherwise → **expensive**

The order of the WHEN clauses matters: check "under 30" before "under 40", otherwise a 25k dish would become "mid-priced".

slides.title: Searched CASE
slides.body: The most common form: each WHEN is a condition.

slides.title: Simple CASE
slides.body: When comparing one column against several fixed values, write it compactly as `CASE cột WHEN giá_trị THEN …`. Use it to map codes to display text.

slides.title: CASE in ORDER BY
slides.body: Sort by **custom order**: coffee first, then tea, then food, not alphabetically.

slides.title: Date and time functions
slides.body: `strftime('%w', …)` returns the day of the week (0 = Sunday), `%H` returns the hour. `date(x, '+7 days')` adds days. `julianday` subtracts two dates to give a number of days.

slides.title: Numbers: rounding and formatting
slides.body: `round(x, n)` rounds to n decimal places; `printf` formats like C: `%,d` adds thousands separators (SQLite 3.38+).

slides.title: Project for stage 2: the menu page
slides.body:
Combine everything you've learned: filter by keyword **and** price range, labels using CASE, sort by custom category then price, pagination.

Change `'%a%'` and the numbers to see how the query responds. This is exactly the SQL query behind the search box of a food-ordering app.

slides.body:
You can now write full read queries on **a single table**: filtering (WHERE, AND/OR, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL), sorting, pagination, and transformations (CASE, string functions, date and time, numeric).

Stage 3: **many rows into one number** (COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY) and **many tables into one result** (JOIN) — answers the question "which dish sells best?"

sql12.summary: Turn many rows into one number with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; distinguish COUNT(*) from COUNT(column); conditional counting.

slides.title: Stage 3: from rows to a single number
slides.body:
The shop owner doesn't want to read individual 120 — they want **one number**: total revenue, number of orders, average cups per order.

Stage 3 has 6 steps: aggregate functions → GROUP BY/HAVING → INNER JOIN → LEFT JOIN and the row-multiplication trap → subqueries → UNION. From this step on, the SQL cell uses **data for the whole month 10**: 12 customers, 120 orders.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 3
slides.body: The left half is **grouping** (aggregate functions, GROUP BY, HAVING), and the right half is **combining** (JOIN, subqueries, UNION). By the end of the stage you can answer "which item sold best this month".

slides.title: Aggregate functions in theory
slides.body:
Codd's original model had no aggregation. Klug (1982) extended relational algebra with the **grouping and aggregation** operator (γ). SQL has been present since the first standardized version, in 1986.

An important property: aggregate functions **ignore NULL** (except COUNT(*)). The AVG of (10, NULL, 20) is 15, not 10.

> Klug, A. (1982) 'Equivalence of relational algebra and relational calculus query languages having aggregate functions', *Journal of the ACM*, 29(3), pp. 699–717.

slides.title: The five numbers the shop owner needs
slides.body:
1. How many orders this month? → COUNT
2. How many cups were sold? → SUM(qty)
3. On average, how many cups per order line? → AVG(qty)
4. When were the first and last orders? → MIN, MAX
5. How many **different** customers have bought? → COUNT(DISTINCT)

slides.title: COUNT(*)
slides.body: Counts every row, including rows with NULL.

slides.title: COUNT(column) skips NULL
slides.body: `COUNT(customer_id)` counts only orders **with** a customer. `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` counts the number of distinct customers.

slides.title: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
slides.body: On the order-line table: total cups, average, minimum, maximum. `round` makes AVG easier to read.

slides.title: MIN/MAX with text and dates
slides.body: MIN and MAX work on text and ISO date-times, because string order matches time order (step 5).

slides.title: Conditional counting
slides.body: Grouping + CASE: count several conditions in **one** scan. SQLite and PostgreSQL also have standard syntax `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …)`.

slides.title: Don't mix plain columns with aggregate functions
slides.body: The statement below is **deliberately wrong** in meaning: `name` sits next to `MAX(price)` without GROUP BY. PostgreSQL raises an error; SQLite has its own exception (taking the row with MAX), but don't rely on it. Step 13 teaches the correct way.

sql12.title: 12. Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

sql13.summary: Group rows into groups with GROUP BY, filter groups with HAVING, and grasp the full processing order of a SELECT statement.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Step 12 gives **one** number for the whole table. The shop owner then asks: the number of orders **per day**, and the number of cups **per item**. That is GROUP BY — one number for **each group**. And HAVING filters the groups: "only the days with more than 5 orders".

slides.title: GROUP BY collapses rows
slides.body: Six items split into three groups by type. Each group becomes **one row** in the result. Columns in SELECT may only be group columns or aggregate functions.

slides.title: Full processing order
slides.body:
The logical order of a SELECT statement under the SQL standard:

1. FROM (and JOIN)
2. WHERE — filter **rows**
3. GROUP BY — group
4. HAVING — filter **groups**
5. SELECT — compute columns
6. ORDER BY
7. LIMIT

> Melton, J. and Simon, A.R. (2002) *SQL:1999 Understanding Relational Language Components*. San Francisco: Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 9.

slides.title: WHERE or HAVING?
slides.body:
- "Morning orders, counted by day" → filter **rows** before grouping → WHERE.
- "Days with more than 5 orders" → filter on the **grouped result** → HAVING.

Rule: a condition with an aggregate function → HAVING; otherwise → WHERE (faster, because it removes rows early).

slides.title: Count items by category
slides.body: One row per category.

slides.title: Orders per day
slides.body: Group by the **expression** `date(ordered_at)`.

slides.title: Group by multiple columns
slides.body: One row per **pair** (item, cups).

slides.title: HAVING filters groups
slides.body: Keep only days with **at least 5 orders**.

slides.title: WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING
slides.body: Orders **with a customer**, grouped by customer, keep the customers who **bought at least 10 orders**, sorted with the most first.

hints: SELECT item_id, SUM(qty) … GROUP BY item_id

quiz.why: Filter rows → group → filter groups → compute columns → sort.

quiz.q: Where does the COUNT(*) > 5 condition go?
quiz.why: A condition on an aggregate function belongs in HAVING.

quiz.q: How many rows? (3 excludes the item)
quiz.why: One row per group.

quiz.q: Filtering with WHERE before GROUP BY is usually faster than filtering the same thing with HAVING.
quiz.why: Remove rows before grouping.

quiz.why: An aggregate function cannot be used in WHERE — move it to HAVING.

quiz.why: HAVING filters groups.

sql14.summary: Join the tables through foreign keys with INNER JOIN, alias the tables, join several tables, and calculate real revenue.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: At this point you only see `item_id = 2` — you can't see item names yet, and you can't calculate money yet. The data lives in **several tables** (step 2). JOIN combines them through foreign keys: an order line + an item = a name and a price; multiply the number of cups and you get **revenue**.

slides.title: Types of JOIN
slides.body: INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that **match on both sides**. LEFT JOIN also keeps the unmatched rows from the left side (step 15). FULL JOIN keeps both sides (SQLite supported from version 3.39).

slides.title: A foreign key is the connecting path
slides.body: `order_items.item_id = menu_items.id` — the exact foreign key arrow you drew in step 2 becomes the ON condition.

slides.title: JOIN is the Cartesian product + selection
slides.body:
In relational algebra, R ⋈ S = σ\_condition(R × S): pair **every** combination of rows, then keep the pairs that satisfy the condition. A DBMS doesn't actually do this (it's too expensive). It uses nested-loop joins with indexes, hash joins or merge joins instead.

> Graefe, G. (1993) 'Query evaluation techniques for large databases', *ACM Computing Surveys*, 25(2), pp. 73–169.

slides.title: Revenue = qty × price
slides.body:
- `order_items`: which order, which item, how many cups.
- `menu_items`: item price.

Join on `item_id = id` → each row has both qty and price → `SUM(qty * price)`.

slides.title: JOIN two tables
slides.body: `ON` states the join condition. Table aliases (`oi`, `m`) keep the query short and make clear which table each column belongs to.

slides.title: Calculate the amount for each line
slides.body: The expression uses columns from both tables.

slides.title: JOIN + GROUP BY: revenue per item
slides.body: Opening question of this stage: **which item sells best in a month**.

slides.title: Joining three tables
slides.body: Customer → order → order line. Each JOIN adds one table.

slides.body: The query below is **intentionally wrong**: both `orders` and `customers` have a column `id` — the DBMS doesn't know which column you mean (`ambiguous column name`). Fix it to `o.id`.

sql15.summary: Keep non-matching rows with LEFT JOIN, find the "missing" ones, self-join a table, and recognize the row-multiplication trap that makes revenue wrong.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: INNER JOIN **drops** non-matching rows: items nobody has ordered, walk-in orders. A report of "every item, including the slow sellers" needs a LEFT JOIN. And a JOIN done the wrong way makes revenue **double** with no error raised.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN
slides.body: LEFT JOIN keeps **every row on the left**; when the right side has no match, its columns are NULL.

slides.title: Anti-join
slides.body:
The pattern "LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL" is called an **anti-join**: it finds left rows **with no** match. The optimizer of PostgreSQL and SQLite recognizes this pattern and runs it efficiently, like NOT EXISTS (step 16).

> PostgreSQL Global Development Group (2025) *PostgreSQL Documentation: Table Expressions — Joined Tables*. Available at: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html

slides.title: "None yet" questions
slides.body:
- Which customers **have never ordered**?
- Which items **nobody has ordered** this week?
- Which orders **have no** customer?

All follow the same pattern: LEFT JOIN then filter the right side with IS NULL.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN keeps walk-in orders
slides.body: Orders 2 and 5 still remain, with the customer name NULL.

slides.title: Count every customer's orders, including 0
slides.body: Count `o.id`, not `*` — `COUNT(*)` would count the NULL row as 1.

slides.body: Add a new item that hasn't sold yet, then find it.

slides.title: Trap: the table condition must go in WHERE
slides.body: To count orders from day 1/10 for **every** customer: putting the date condition in WHERE drops customers with 0 orders (because o.ordered_at NULL), which turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER. Correct: put it in **ON**.

slides.title: Row-multiplication trap
slides.body: Joining **two child tables** of the same parent multiplies rows. Here order 3 has 2 line items, and JOIN adds the payments table with 2 payments → 4 rows, so the total is **doubled**. Fix: aggregate each child table in a subquery first, then JOIN (step 16).

slides.title: Self-join
slides.body: A table joined with **itself** through two aliases. Example: pairs of items in the same category.

sql16.summary: Nesting queries inside queries: scalar subqueries, IN, EXISTS, correlated subqueries, and subqueries in FROM.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: The result of SELECT is a table (step 3), so it can be placed **inside** another statement. "Items priced above the average" requires knowing the average first: that is a subquery.

slides.title: Three places to put a subquery
slides.body:
| Location | Returns | Example |
|---|---|---|
| WHERE x > (…) | **one value** | price > average price |
| WHERE x IN (…) | **one column** | customers who ever bought tea |
| FROM (…) AS t | **one table** | aggregate first, then JOIN |

slides.title: EXISTS and semi-joins
slides.body:
`EXISTS (truy vấn con)` is a **semi-join**: it only asks "does at least one row exist?" and stops as soon as it finds one. `NOT EXISTS` is safe with NULL — unlike `NOT IN` (step 9).

> Date, C.J. (2015) *SQL and Relational Theory*. 3rd edn. O'Reilly, ch. 10.

slides.title: Split the problem into two steps
slides.body:
"Items priced above average":

1. What is the average price? → `SELECT AVG(price) FROM menu_items`
2. Which items have a price > that number?

Write step 1 on its own, run it, then wrap it in parentheses and place it into step 2.

slides.title: Scalar subquery
slides.body: Returns exactly **one** value — used as a single number.

slides.title: IN with a subquery
slides.body: Customers who ever ordered **tea**: get the list of orders containing a tea item → the list of customers.

slides.title: Correlated EXISTS
slides.body: The subquery **references the outer table** (`c.id`) — it runs again for each customer. Here: customers who have at least one order.

slides.title: Subquery in FROM
slides.body: Aggregate first, join after — the fix for the row-multiplication trap in step 15. The temporary table `t` has one row per order.

slides.title: Subqueries in SELECT
slides.body: Each dish shows how many times it was ordered. A correlated subquery returns one value per row.

slides.title: Exercise 1: cheapest dish
slides.body: Show the dish names whose price is **equal to the lowest price**.

slides.title: Exercise 2: customers who have not bought (NOT EXISTS)
slides.body: Use **NOT EXISTS** to show customers with no orders (the initial sample data already added 1 new customers).

hints: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)

slides.title: Exercise 3: orders above average
slides.body: Show `order_id` the orders whose **total is greater than the average total of all orders** (monthly data).

hints: Step 1: temporary table of the total for each order.
Step 2: compare against the AVG of that same temporary table (step 28 teaches CTE so you don't have to repeat it).

quiz.q: A subquery placed after WHERE price > (…) must return what?
quiz.why: A scalar subquery.

quiz.q: NOT EXISTS is safer with NULL than NOT IN.
quiz.why: NOT IN returns no rows if NULL appears in the list.

quiz.q: What is a correlated subquery?
o: It references columns of the outer query and re-runs for each row
quiz.why: Example: WHERE o.customer_id = c.id.

quiz.q: Completes a semi-join.
quiz.why: EXISTS only asks whether something exists.

quiz.q: How do you fix the row-multiplication trap?
o: Aggregate each child table in a subquery at FROM, then JOIN
quiz.why: Each child table still has one row per key before joining.

sql16.title: 16. Subqueries, IN, EXISTS

sql17.summary: Combine, intersect and subtract the results of two queries using set operations; distinguish UNION and UNION ALL.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: JOIN combines **horizontally** (adds columns). Set operations combine **vertically** (adds rows): a list of customers who bought in the morning **and** in the afternoon, and customers who bought in the morning **but not** in the afternoon.

slides.title: Venn diagram
slides.body: The circles are now two **query results**. UNION = the shaded part of FULL, INTERSECT = the middle, EXCEPT = the left part minus the middle.

slides.title: Set theory
slides.body:
Union, intersection and difference are the three operations of Cantor's set theory, which Codd carried directly into relational algebra. Condition: the two relations must be **compatible**, with the same number of columns and matching types.

> Codd, E.F. (1970) 'A relational model of data for large shared data banks', *Communications of the ACM*, 13(6), pp. 377–387.

slides.title: Morning and afternoon customers
slides.body: Two queries: customers with orders before 12h, and customers with orders from 12h. The question "customers who came to both sessions" is an **intersection**; "only came in the morning" is a **difference**.

slides.title: UNION removes duplicates
slides.body: Merges two lists so each value appears once.

slides.title: UNION ALL keeps duplicates, and it is faster
slides.body: It does not remove duplicates, so no sorting or hashing is needed. Use UNION ALL when you know there are no duplicates or when you need to count.

slides.title: INTERSECT
slides.body: Customers who came **both** in the morning and in the afternoon.

slides.title: EXCEPT
slides.body: Dishes on the menu **minus** the dishes already sold.

slides.title: ORDER BY placed last
slides.body: A set query has only **one** ORDER BY at the end, applied to the whole result.

slides.title: Exercise 1: shared contact list
slides.body: One column containing **dish names and customer names**, without duplicates.

hints: Two SELECT with the same 1 name column.

slides.title: Exercise 2: afternoon only
slides.body: With the initial sample data: `customer_id` of customers who have **only** orders from 12h onward and no morning orders.

slides.title: Stage 3 summary
slides.body: You can now answer "which dish sells best", "which customers are loyal" and "which hours are busy" using GROUP BY, JOIN, subqueries and set operations. Stage 4: **design** the database yourself, because no matter how elegant a query is, it cannot rescue a wrong schema.

quiz.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
o: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them
quiz.why: UNION ALL is faster because it does not remove duplicates.

quiz.q: Both sides of a UNION must have the same number of columns.
quiz.why: Compatible relations.

quiz.q: Match each operation with its meaning.
quiz.why: The three set operations.

quiz.q: Where does ORDER BY go in a UNION statement?
quiz.why: Applies to the whole result.

quiz.q: Dishes on the menu but not yet sold.
quiz.why: Set difference.
