sql18.summary: Read and draw entity–relationship diagrams (ERD): entities, attributes, relationships and cardinality 1–1, 1–n, n–n.

slides.title: Stage 4: design first, write later
slides.body:
Shop Hạt opens a second branch, adds menu categories, and adds the labels "less sugar" and "vegan". A four-table schema is no longer enough.

Stage 4: ERD → CREATE TABLE and keys → constraints → normalization → many-to-many relationships. Wrap-up: a schema of 8 tables that reaches **3NF**.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 4
slides.body: Eight branches, three layers: **model** (ERD, many-to-many relationships), **keys and constraints**, **normalization**. The three layers answer three questions: what to store, how to block bad data, and where to store it so it isn't duplicated.

slides.title: ERD of shop Hạt (target version)
slides.body: Eight tables. Arrows go from the foreign key to the primary key. Dashed line: `item_tags` is the **junction table** of the many-to-many relationship between dishes and labels (step 22).

slides.title: Chen's entity–relationship model
slides.body:
Peter Chen (1976) proposed drawing data with **entities** (rectangles), **relationships** (diamonds) and **attributes** (ellipses), before choosing a DBMS. Today the crow's foot notation of Gordon Everest is more common, and more compact.

> Chen, P.P. (1976) 'The entity-relationship model — toward a unified view of data', *ACM TODS*, 1(1), pp. 9–36.

slides.title: Finding entities from a description
slides.body:
The shop owner says: "Each **branch** sells from the same **menu**. A **dish** belongs to one **category** and can have several **labels**. A **customer** places an **order** at one branch; an order has several dishes."

The nouns in bold are entity candidates. Verbs ("belongs", "places", "has") are relationships.

slides.title: Three kinds of cardinality
slides.body:
| Relationship | Example | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 – 1 | customer – membership card | foreign key with UNIQUE |
| 1 – n | branch – order | foreign key on the n side |
| n – n | dish – label | junction table |

Ask both directions: "How many orders does one branch have?" → many. "How many branches does one order belong to?" → one. So it is 1 – n.

slides.title: Weak entity
slides.body: `order_items` has no meaning without its order: it is a **weak entity**, and its key consists of the parent entity's key (`order_id`) plus its own part (`item_id`). When an order is deleted, its line items must go too (step 19: ON DELETE CASCADE).

slides.title: Read an existing schema
slides.body: SQLite stores the schema in the system table `sqlite_schema`. This is how you read the ERD of a database you have never seen.

slides.title: PRAGMA foreign_key_list
slides.body: Lists the foreign keys of a table. These are exactly the arrows on the ERD.

slides.title: Exercise: list tables
slides.body: Show the **name** of every table in the database (name column only).

slides.title: Practice: draw an ERD on paper
slides.body:
Draw an ERD for this scenario: "A shop has **staff**; each order is taken by one cashier; a staff member works at one branch; each branch has a manager (who is also staff)."

Hint: the "manager" relationship is 1 – 1 from branch to staff, and it creates a loop between the two tables.

quiz.q: Who proposed the entity-relationship model (1976)?
quiz.why: Peter Chen, ACM TODS 1976.

quiz.q: Mapping relationships to implementation.
pairs: foreign key on the n side
quiz.why: Three kinds of cardinality.

quiz.q: Dish – label (one dish has many labels, one label has many dishes) is?
quiz.why: Needs the junction table item_tags.

quiz.q: A weak entity has a key that contains its parent entity's key.
quiz.why: order_items: (order_id, item_id).

quiz.q: The system table holds the SQLite schema.
quiz.why: Old name: sqlite_master.

sql18.title: 18. Entity–relationship diagram (ERD)

sql19.summary: Create tables with CREATE TABLE, declare primary keys, foreign keys with ON DELETE, change the schema with ALTER TABLE, and drop with DROP.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Turn the ERD into real tables: `CREATE TABLE`, primary keys, foreign keys, the behavior when the parent is deleted (`ON DELETE`), then `ALTER TABLE` to add a column to a table that already has data.

slides.title: Schema to build
slides.body: This step builds `branches` and links `orders` to it. `categories`, `tags`, `item_tags` are saved for steps 21–22.

slides.title: Referential integrity
slides.body:
The SQL-92 standard defines five actions when a parent row is deleted or updated: `NO ACTION`, `RESTRICT`, `CASCADE`, `SET NULL`, `SET DEFAULT`. Choosing wrong either loses data (CASCADE deletes the whole order history by mistake) or leaves data stuck (RESTRICT blocks closing a branch).

> ISO/IEC (1992) *ISO/IEC 9075:1992*, §11.8 <referential constraint definition>.

slides.title: What if a branch is closed?
slides.body:
- Delete all the branch's orders? → **No**: loses historical revenue.
- Block deletion while orders remain? → `RESTRICT` — safe.
- Or keep the orders and set the branch to NULL? → `SET NULL` — loses track of where the order information goes.

For money: **RESTRICT** and "mark as closed" instead of deleting.

slides.title: CREATE TABLE
slides.body: Table name, then the column list (name, type, constraints). `STRICT` enforces strict types such as PostgreSQL.

slides.title: STRICT rejects wrong types
slides.body: The query below is **deliberately wrong**: in a STRICT table, text cannot go into an INTEGER column.

slides.title: Foreign key with ON DELETE
slides.body: `order_items` follows the order (CASCADE); an order blocks deleting a branch that still has data (RESTRICT). Try `DELETE FROM branches WHERE id = 1;` after running it.

slides.title: ALTER TABLE adds column
slides.body: Add `branch_id` to `orders` that already has data. SQLite does not allow adding a foreign-key column with a DEFAULT other than NULL, so do it in two steps: add the column allowing NULL, then UPDATE to assign a branch to the old orders.

slides.title: DROP TABLE
slides.body: Deletes both the table and its data, and this cannot be undone. `IF EXISTS` avoids errors when the table does not exist.

slides.title: Exercise 1: category table
slides.body: Create table `categories(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)`, add 3 rows `(1,'coffee'), (2,'tea'), (3,'food')`, then `SELECT * FROM categories;`

hints: Tick the checkbox for the result of the last SELECT statement.

slides.title: Exercise 2: add a notes column
slides.body: Add column `note TEXT` to `customers`, then show `name, note` for every customer.

hints: The new column defaults to NULL.

quiz.q: Deleting an order also deletes its line items. Which one should we use?
quiz.why: A weak entity follows its parent.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't orders CASCADE from their branch?
quiz.why: Money and history must be kept. Use RESTRICT.

quiz.q: A STRICT table accepts the string 'ten' in an INTEGER column.
quiz.why: STRICT raises a type error.

quiz.q: Adding columns to an existing table.
quiz.why: ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN.

quiz.q: Which ON DELETE behavior is valid under the standard?
quiz.why: Five behaviors: NO ACTION, RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT.

sql19.title: 19. CREATE TABLE, primary keys and foreign keys

sql20.summary: Let the database block bad data with NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT and generated columns.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Application code can forget to check; the database **never forgets**. Constraints are the last line of defense: negative prices, duplicate phone numbers, orders without a time. All of them are blocked on the spot.

slides.title: Constraints in the mind map
slides.body: The **Constraints** branch of step 4: NOT NULL (required), UNIQUE (no duplicates), CHECK (condition), DEFAULT (default value).

slides.title: Integrity at the data layer
slides.body:
The principle of 'putting rules as close to the data as possible' is emphasized in database design texts: rules in the DBMS apply to **every** application, script and user, while rules in code apply only to that code.

> Elmasri, R. and Navathe, S.B. (2016) *Fundamentals of Database Systems*. 7th edn. Pearson, ch. 5.

slides.title: Business rules of Hạt
slides.body:
- The menu item must have a name; price > 0 and ≤ 500.000.
- Customer phone numbers must be unique (but may be left blank).
- Number of cups from 1 to 50.
- The order time defaults to the time it is created.

Each line is one constraint.

slides.title: CHECK
slides.body: The second INSERT statement is **intentionally wrong** (it violates a constraint). Read the `CHECK constraint failed` error.

slides.title: UNIQUE and NULL
slides.body: UNIQUE allows **multiple NULL** (NULL is not equal to NULL — step 9). That's the intent: many customers without a phone number are still allowed.

slides.title: DEFAULT
slides.body: If a column is not written, it takes its default value, including expressions such as the current time.

slides.title: Generated columns
slides.body: `GENERATED ALWAYS AS` is computed from other columns, so it is always correct and no one can edit it by hand. Example: a lowercase name for searching (step 8).

slides.title: Multi-column constraints
slides.body: Written after the column list: UNIQUE across a pair of columns, CHECK comparing two columns.

slides.title: Exercise: a safe order line items table
slides.body: Create table `lines(order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (qty BETWEEN 1 AND 50))`, insert `(1, 2)`, then `SELECT * FROM lines;`

quiz.q: A UNIQUE column in SQLite allows multiple NULL rows.
quiz.why: NULL is not equal to NULL.

quiz.q: Block negative prices with?
quiz.why: CHECK tests a condition.

quiz.q: Defaults to the creation time.
quiz.why: DEFAULT (expression).

quiz.q: What is the advantage of a GENERATED column?
o: Always matches the source column and cannot be edited by hand
quiz.why: One source of truth.

quiz.q: Why enforce rules in the DBMS instead of only in code?
o: Applies to every app, script, and user
quiz.why: The last line of defense.

sql20.title: 20. Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT

sql21.summary: Recognize duplicated data and update anomalies, then normalize a flat table into 3NF.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: An Excel sheet with "everything in one" looks convenient, until Lan changes her phone number and you have to edit 30 rows. Miss 1 row and the data contradicts itself. **Normalization** is the process of splitting tables so each fact lives in only one place.

slides.title: The Three Normal Forms
slides.body: Each higher normal form includes the previous one. In practice, **3NF** is the target of most designs.

slides.title: Codd 1971 and Kent's mnemonic
slides.body:
Codd (1971) defined 2NF and 3NF based on **functional dependencies**: A → B means knowing A tells you exactly B. William Kent (1983) summed it up with a mnemonic: *every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key*.

> Codd, E.F. (1971) 'Further normalization of the data base relational model', IBM Research Report RJ909.
>
> Kent, W. (1983) 'A simple guide to five normal forms in relational database theory', *Communications of the ACM*, 26(2), pp. 120–125.

slides.title: Three Anomalies
slides.body:
With the flat table `flat_orders`:

- **Update anomaly**: changing Lan's number requires editing many rows.
- **Insert anomaly**: you cannot add a new menu item until someone orders it.
- **Delete anomaly**: deleting the only order with Matcha also deletes the price of Matcha.

slides.title: Flat table
slides.body: Minh's name and phone number repeat 3 times, and the price of Peach Tea repeats 2 times.

slides.title: 1NF: one value per cell
slides.body: The table is 1NF: no cell holds a list. (Violating version: column `items = 'cà phê, bánh mì'`.) The key of the flat table is **(order_id, item_name)**.

slides.title: 2NF: full-key dependency
slides.body: `customer_name` depends only on `order_id`, which is **part** of the key, so it violates 2NF. Move order information into its own table.

slides.title: 3NF: no transitive dependency
slides.body: In the orders table: `order_id → customer_phone → customer_name`. The name depends on the key **through** the phone number, which violates 3NF. Move customers into their own table.

slides.title: Result: four familiar tables
slides.body: After splitting, you have the customers – orders – order_items – menu_items schema from step 2. The schema of Hạt was already 3NF; now you know **why**.

slides.title: When to denormalize
slides.body: Read-heavy, write-light reports sometimes **deliberately** store duplicates. For example, the price at time of sale in the order line means changing the menu price doesn't corrupt old receipts. That is an intentional design decision, not a design error.

slides.title: Exercise: split the menu table
slides.body: From `flat_orders`, take the list of **distinct dishes** with the two columns name and price.

quiz.q: What is an update anomaly?
o: Must fix the same fact in many rows
quiz.why: Missing one row causes a contradiction.

quiz.q: Which normal form order?
quiz.why: Each form includes the one before it.

quiz.q: Does customer_name depend only on order_id within the key (order_id, item_name)? Is that a violation?
quiz.why: Partial dependency on the key.

quiz.q: Storing the sale price in the order line is a deliberate denormalization.
quiz.why: Changing the menu price does not make old invoices wrong.

quiz.q: Kent's memory aid: depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but ___

sql21.title: 21. Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF

sql22.summary: Implementing many-to-many relationships with a junction table, two-way queries, and completing the schema of the 8 tables of Hạt.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: A dish can have many labels ("less sugar", "vegan"), and one label can apply to many dishes. You cannot put a foreign key on either side, so you need a **third table**.

slides.title: The item_tags junction table
slides.body: Bottom right: `menu_items` ← `item_tags` → `tags`. The junction table has only two foreign keys, and its primary key is the **pair** of them.

slides.title: Why not store the list in a single column
slides.body:
The `tags = 'ít đường,thuần chay'` column violates 1NF: you cannot set a foreign key on it, you cannot count "how many vegan dishes" with GROUP BY, and renaming a label means fixing the string everywhere. Karwin calls this the **Jaywalking** antipattern.

> Karwin, B. (2010) *SQL Antipatterns*. Raleigh: Pragmatic Bookshelf, ch. 2.

slides.title: Two-way questions
slides.body: "What tags does Peach Tea have?" (dish → tags) and "Which dishes are vegan?" (tag → dishes). Both are **two-way JOIN** through the junction table.

slides.title: Dish → tags
slides.body: Tags of Peach Tea (id 2): go from the junction table to the tags table.

slides.title: Tag → dishes
slides.body: Vegan dishes.

slides.title: Combine the tags into one string for display
slides.body: `group_concat` concatenates the tags for **display**; storage still keeps them in separate tables.

slides.title: Dishes that have BOTH tags
slides.body: "Low sugar **and** vegan": filter on the two tags, then keep the dishes that have all of the 2. This is the familiar **relational division** operation.

slides.title: Exercise 1: count dishes per tag
slides.body: Show the tag name and the **number of dishes** that carry it.

slides.title: Exercise 2: new dishes
slides.body: Show the names of the dishes that carry the `mới` tag.

hints: Two JOIN through a junction table.

slides.title: Stage 4 summary
slides.body: You have gone from the shop owner's description → ERD → CREATE TABLE with keys and constraints → normalization to 3NF → many-to-many relationships. Stage 5: **writing** data safely — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE inside a transaction, and blocking SQL Injection.

quiz.q: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented?
o: A foreign key on one side
A junction table with two foreign keys
quiz.why: item_tags(item_id, tag_id).

quiz.q: Storing 'less sugar,vegan' in a single column is good design.
quiz.why: An anti-pattern called Jaywalking, violating 1NF.

quiz.q: Concatenate the labels for display.
quiz.why: PostgreSQL uses string_agg.

quiz.q: What is the primary key of a junction table usually?
quiz.why: Prevents attaching the same tag twice.

quiz.q: Which dish has BOTH tags: which query?
o: IN (a, b) + GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(*) = 2
quiz.why: Each row holds only one tag name; count up to 2.

sql22.title: 22. Many-to-many relationships and junction tables

sql23.summary: Insert, update and delete data correctly: multi-row INSERT and INSERT … SELECT, conditional UPDATE and UPDATE using values from other tables, and safe DELETE.

slides.title: Stage 5: writing data safely
slides.body:
Reading wrong only makes reports wrong; **writing wrong loses real data**. Stage 5: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE → UPSERT, RETURNING → transaction ACID → view, trigger → SQL Injection.

All SQL cells still run on their own copy: delete freely, and click **Reset** to return to the original state.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 5
slides.body: The three branches above are the three basic write commands; the remaining branches are **safe** ways to write: merging, transactions, automation and parameterization.

slides.title: Rule: "SELECT first, then write"
slides.body:
The most classic data incident is `UPDATE`/`DELETE` **forgetting WHERE**. The safe practice that operations teams recommend: write the SELECT statement with that same WHERE, check the row count, and only then change SELECT to UPDATE/DELETE, always inside a transaction (step 25).

> Kleppmann, M. (2017) *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*. Sebastopol: O'Reilly, ch. 7.

slides.title: The cashier's three tasks
slides.body:
1. A customer orders a drink → **INSERT** an order and an order line.
2. Raise the price of Peach tea to 2.000đ → **UPDATE**.
3. Cancel a mistaken order → **DELETE** (or better: mark it as cancelled).

slides.title: INSERT names the columns
slides.body: Always list the columns: adding a column to the table later will not break the INSERT. If you omit `id`, `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` assigns it automatically.

slides.title: INSERT … SELECT
slides.body: Copy query results into a table, e.g. saving a daily summary.

slides.title: Conditional UPDATE
slides.body: Raise the price of peach tea by 2.000đ. Run SELECT with the same WHERE first to make sure it matches the right rows.

slides.title: UPDATE from another table
slides.body: `UPDATE … FROM` (SQLite 3.33+, PostgreSQL): write the total cups sold into the new column.

slides.title: DELETE and soft delete
slides.body: Hard deletion leaves no trace. Payment systems usually use **soft delete**: add a `cancelled_at` column, and filter out `WHERE cancelled_at IS NULL` rows when reading.

slides.title: Exercise 1: new item
slides.body: Add the `Bạc xỉu muối` item, category `coffee`, price `35000`; then show the name and price of all `coffee` items.

hints: INSERT INTO menu_items (name, category, price) VALUES (…);
End with SELECT so the cell can be graded.

slides.title: Exercise 2: food discount
slides.body: Reduce the price of every `food` item by **10%** (rounded to an integer), then show `name, price` of the food item.

slides.title: Exercise 3: delete a line item
slides.body: Delete **banh mi** (item 4) from order 3, then show all lines of order 3.

hints: WHERE must include both order_id and item_id.
Forgetting WHERE deletes the entire table!

quiz.q: What does UPDATE menu_items SET price = 0; (without WHERE) do?
quiz.why: Without WHERE it applies to the whole table.

quiz.q: Listing the columns in INSERT keeps the statement stable when the table gains columns.
quiz.why: It does not depend on column position.

quiz.q: What is soft delete?
o: Mark a cancelled_at column instead of deleting the row
quiz.why: Keeps an audit trail for accounting; can be recovered.

quiz.q: Copies query results into a table.
quiz.why: INSERT … SELECT.

quiz.q: What is the safe data-fixing procedure?
items: Switch to UPDATE inside a transaction
quiz.why: SELECT first, then write.

sql23.title: 23. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

sql24.summary: Insert-or-update in one statement with INSERT … ON CONFLICT, and retrieve the just-written data with RETURNING.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: A customer adds another Bac xiu to an order that already has Bac xiu: a second row cannot be inserted (duplicate primary key), so you must **add to the cup count**. "Update if it exists, insert if it doesn't" is called **UPSERT**.

slides.title: UPSERT in the diagram
slides.body: The UPSERT branch sits between INSERT and UPDATE: one statement, one pass, with no gap for two cashiers to cut in.

slides.title: Why not "SELECT then INSERT"
slides.body:
A two-step SELECT-then-INSERT has a **race condition**: two requests both see "not present", both INSERT, and one fails on a duplicate key. The atomic UPSERT solves this in one statement. PostgreSQL has ON CONFLICT since 9.5, SQLite since 3.24, and the SQL standard uses MERGE.

> PostgreSQL Global Development Group (2025) *INSERT — ON CONFLICT Clause*. Available at: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html

slides.title: Add an item to the order
slides.body: Order 1 already has 2 Bac xiu. The customer orders 1 more → expect 3, still **one** row.

slides.title: Duplicate key error
slides.body: The statement below is **intentionally wrong**: (1, 1) already exists.

slides.title: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
slides.body: `excluded` is the row being inserted that got blocked. Add its cup count to the existing row.

slides.title: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
slides.body: Skip if it already exists: handy when importing repeated data without wanting errors.

slides.title: RETURNING
slides.body: Retrieve the row just written within the **same** statement, with no need for an extra SELECT (and nobody can cut in). Useful for getting the newly assigned id.

slides.title: UPDATE … RETURNING
slides.body: See the new price right after the edit.

slides.title: Exercise 1: add cups
slides.body: Order 3 customer orders **2 black coffees** (item 3). Use UPSERT, then show the `(3, 3)` row.

slides.title: Exercise 2: new item and id
slides.body: Add the `Trà vải` item, category `tea`, price `38000` and return **id, name** using RETURNING.

hints: RETURNING at the end of the INSERT statement.

quiz.q: What does UPSERT mean?
o: Update if it exists, insert if it doesn't, in one statement
quiz.why: INSERT … ON CONFLICT.

quiz.q: What is the blocked row being inserted called?
quiz.why: The virtual table excluded.

quiz.q: SELECT checks, then INSERT can fail when two requests run at the same time.
quiz.why: Race condition.

quiz.q: What is RETURNING used for?
o: Return the data of the row just written
quiz.why: Example: the just-assigned id.

quiz.q: What is UPSERT called in the SQL standard?
quiz.why: MERGE; PostgreSQL/SQLite use ON CONFLICT.

sql24.title: 24. UPSERT and RETURNING

sql25.summary: Group several write statements into one transaction with BEGIN … COMMIT/ROLLBACK, and understand the four ACID properties, SAVEPOINT, and isolation levels.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Placing an order takes **three** steps: create the order, add the order lines, and subtract stock. A power cut after the second step leaves an order with no stock deducted. A transaction guarantees: **all three or nothing**.

slides.title: The four ACID properties
slides.body: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

slides.title: Origins of ACID
slides.body:
Jim Gray (1981) laid the conceptual foundation for transactions; Härder and Reuter (1983) coined the acronym ACID. Gray received the Turing Award 1998 for his work on transactions.

> Gray, J. (1981) 'The transaction concept: virtues and limitations', *Proceedings of VLDB 1981*, pp. 144–154.
>
> Härder, T. and Reuter, A. (1983) 'Principles of transaction-oriented database recovery', *ACM Computing Surveys*, 15(4), pp. 287–317.

slides.title: Placing an order safely
slides.body: BEGIN → add order → add lines → subtract stock. If stock goes negative (CHECK blocks it) → ROLLBACK the whole order. If everything is fine → COMMIT. A half-finished state never exists.

slides.title: BEGIN … COMMIT
slides.body: Three write statements form one unit.

slides.title: ROLLBACK cancels everything
slides.body: After ROLLBACK, order 10 does not exist — as if it never ran.

slides.title: Constraints + transactions
slides.body: Only 1 cups of peach tea are left. The second UPDATE statement is **deliberately wrong** — it violates CHECK → the application must ROLLBACK. Run it, then check the stock table: is item row 2 still 1? This cell stops at the error and the transaction is still open — in a real application, the error-handling code would call ROLLBACK.

slides.title: SAVEPOINT
slides.body: A save point inside a transaction: roll back part of the work without cancelling everything.

slides.title: Isolation levels
slides.body:
The SQL standard defines four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Lower levels are faster but allow "dirty reads", "non-repeatable reads", and "phantoms".

- **SQLite**: default is SERIALIZABLE (one writer at a time).
- **PostgreSQL**: default is READ COMMITTED.

> Berenson, H. et al. (1995) 'A critique of ANSI SQL isolation levels', *Proceedings of ACM SIGMOD 1995*, pp. 1–10.

slides.title: Exercise: place the whole order
slides.body: In **one transaction**: create order `id 11` for customer 3 at `'2026-10-03 11:00'`, add 1 Matcha (item 5)… but Matcha stock = 0! ROLLBACK, then prove order 11 **does not** exist: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE id = 11;`

hints: BEGIN … ROLLBACK cancels everything in between.

quiz.q: Match each letter to a property.
pairs: does not see another transaction's unfinished work
quiz.why: ACID.

quiz.q: What does ROLLBACK do?
quiz.why: Atomicity.

quiz.q: Rolls back to a point in the middle of the transaction.
quiz.why: Full syntax: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name (the SAVEPOINT keyword is optional).

quiz.q: What is the default isolation level of PostgreSQL?
quiz.why: SQLite defaults to SERIALIZABLE.

quiz.q: Who coined the name ACID (1983)?
quiz.why: Gray laid the conceptual foundation for transactions (1981).

sql25.title: 25. Transactions and ACID

sql26.summary: Name a frequently used query with a VIEW, automate writes with a TRIGGER, and know when not to use a trigger.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: The JOIN query that calculates order totals, which you keep rewriting from stage 3. A **view** saves it as a "virtual table". A **trigger** makes the DBMS do work automatically when a write happens — for example, logging every price change.

slides.title: Views and triggers in the diagram
slides.body: A VIEW is the compact **read** layer; a TRIGGER is the automatic **write** layer. Both live inside the database, so every application shares them.

slides.title: Views and data independence
slides.body:
Views implement Codd's **logical data independence**: change the underlying table structure, keep the view unchanged, and the application needs no changes. Use triggers sparingly — logic hidden inside the DBMS is hard to debug; Karwin advises using them only for logging and integrity.

> ANSI/X3/SPARC (1975) *Interim Report: Study Group on Data Base Management Systems*. FDT Bulletin 7(2).

slides.title: The shop owner's two needs
slides.body:
1. A "table" `order_totals(order_id, tien)` that is always correct, used for every report.
2. Every time a dish price changes, record the old price, the new price, and when — for reconciliation.

slides.title: CREATE VIEW
slides.body: Query a view just like a table.

slides.title: Views are always up to date
slides.body: A view does not store data — every read reruns the query. After changing prices, reading the view again shows the new numbers.

slides.title: TRIGGER that logs prices
slides.body: `AFTER UPDATE OF price`: runs after every update to the price column. `OLD` and `NEW` are the row before/after.

slides.title: TRIGGER that blocks a business rule
slides.body: `RAISE(ABORT, …)` cancels the statement. The final UPDATE is **deliberately wrong**: raising the price above 50% is blocked.

slides.title: Exercise 1: regulars view
slides.body: Create a view `regulars` containing `customer_id` and `so_don` of customers with **at least 2 orders**, then `SELECT * FROM regulars;`

hints: CREATE VIEW regulars AS SELECT … GROUP BY … HAVING …

slides.title: Exercise 2: count through the view
slides.body: Using the `order_totals` view (already created), count the orders with a total **of 50.000 or more**.

hints: Use the view like a table.

quiz.q: A view stores a copy of the data at creation time.
quiz.why: A view reruns its query on every read (a materialized view is different).

quiz.q: In a trigger, what is the row before the change called?
quiz.why: OLD and NEW.

quiz.q: Cancel the statement inside a trigger.
quiz.why: RAISE(ABORT, message).

quiz.q: When should you use a trigger?
quiz.why: Hidden logic is hard to debug — use sparingly.

quiz.q: What does a view contribute to data independence?
o: Change the underlying table while the app still reads the view as before
quiz.why: Logical data independence.

sql26.title: 26. Views, triggers and generated columns

sql27.summary: Understand how SQL Injection works, try it yourself on a copy, and stop it at the root with parameterized statements and least privilege.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: The app's search box pastes what the user types directly into the SQL statement. Typing a single quote **changes the meaning of the statement**. That is SQL Injection, a vulnerability that has sat in the OWASP Top 10 for two decades.

slides.title: Parameterization in the diagram
slides.body: The **?** branch is a parameter placeholder. Data travels its own path and never becomes SQL code.

slides.title: OWASP
slides.body:
OWASP ranks Injection in category A03 (2021). The number-one measure in OWASP's cheat sheet: **prepared statements with parameterized queries**, not character filtering and not manual escaping.

> OWASP Foundation (2021) *OWASP Top 10: A03 Injection*. Available at: https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/ (CC BY-SA 4.0).

slides.title: String-concatenated SQL statement
slides.body:
App code (pseudocode):

~~~js
db.exec("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE phone = '" + input + "'");
~~~

If `input` is `' OR '1'='1`, the statement becomes `… WHERE phone = '' OR '1'='1'`. **Every** customer appears.

slides.title: Try the attack yourself
slides.body: This is the SQL statement **after** the app concatenates the malicious input. Run it and the whole contacts list is exposed. (A copy in the browser, it affects no one.)

slides.title: UNION-style Injection
slides.body: The attacker appends a UNION to read a **different** table. Here, it reads the entire schema.

slides.title: Parameterized statement
Table and column names cannot be parameterized
slides.body: `?` only substitutes **values**. Column names for sorting (`ORDER BY ?`) must go through an **allowlist** in the code: accept only `'price'`, `'name'`.

slides.title: Defense in depth
slides.body:
- Parameterize **every** query.
- The app's DB account has minimal privileges (no DROP, no reading system tables).
- Do not return raw SQL error messages to users.
- Log unusual queries.

slides.title: Exercise: signs of an attack
slides.body: The `access_log(q TEXT)` table stores what users typed. Find the rows **containing a single quote** (a sign of an injection attempt).

hints: In a SQL string, a single quote is written as two: ''

slides.title: Stage 5 summary
slides.body: You can write data correctly (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, UPSERT), completely (ACID transactions), automatically (views, triggers) and safely (parameterized queries). Stage 6: **advanced queries**, meaning CTE and window functions, the topics employers test most often.

quiz.q: How do you stop SQL Injection at the root?
quiz.why: OWASP: the number-one measure.

quiz.q: How many customers does the following statement return? (4 customers)
quiz.why: '1'='1' is always true.

quiz.q: You can use ? to parameterize column names in ORDER BY.
quiz.why: Only values can be substituted; column names use an allowlist.

quiz.q: What does least privilege for the app's database account mean?
o: Only the permissions the app needs
quiz.why: Limits the damage if attacked.

quiz.q: Which defense layers are correct?
quiz.why: Concatenating strings is the cause, not the defense.

sql27.title: 27. SQL Injection and parameterized queries

sql28.summary: Name each step of a complex query with WITH (CTE), reuse a step several times, and read the query from top to bottom.

slides.title: Stage 6: advanced queries
slides.body:
The 3 exercise in step 16 asks you to write **the same subquery twice**. CTE (Common Table Expression) names it once, and it can be used as many times as needed.

Stage 6: CTE → recursive CTE → ROW_NUMBER/RANK → LAG/LEAD → running totals and window frames. This is the part that **SQL interviews** ask about most.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 6
slides.body: The first two branches are **CTE** (how the query is organized); the next five are **window functions** (calculations across rows without collapsing them).

slides.title: CTE in the SQL standard:1999
slides.body:
The WITH clause entered the SQL:1999 standard, together with recursive queries. Besides readability, CTE allows **step-by-step testing**: run each CTE on its own to see the intermediate results.

> Melton, J. and Simon, A.R. (2002) *SQL:1999 Understanding Relational Language Components*. Morgan Kaufmann, ch. 12.

slides.title: Write queries like writing a recipe
slides.body:
1. `order_totals`: amount per order.
2. `avg_total`: average of step 1.
3. Result: orders above average.

Each step gets a name and is read from top to bottom, like a cooking recipe.

slides.title: Basic WITH
slides.body: CTE only lasts for **one** statement.

slides.title: Chaining several CTE
slides.body: A later CTE can reference an earlier CTE. The hard exercise in step 16 is now much tidier.

slides.title: Using one CTE twice
slides.body: Compare daily revenue with the best day — using the same `daily` twice.

slides.title: CTE and performance
slides.body: SQLite and PostgreSQL 12+ can "inline" CTE into the main query to optimize. To force it to be computed once and reused: `WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (…)`.

slides.title: Exercise 1: days above average
slides.body: Use CTE `daily(ngay, so_don)` to count orders per day, then show **the days with more orders than average**.

slides.title: Exercise 2: highest-spending customers
slides.body: CTE `spend(customer_id, tien)` = total amount per customer (excluding walk-in customers). Show **the customer with the highest total** (customer_id, tien).

quiz.q: Which keyword is used to declare CTE?
quiz.why: WITH name AS (…).

quiz.q: A later CTE can use CTE declared before it in the same WITH.
quiz.why: Chained, like steps.

quiz.q: What is the scope of CTE?
quiz.why: Unlike a temp table or a view.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of CTE?
o: Readable, reusable, and testable step by step
quiz.why: Organizes the query.

quiz.q: Forces CTE to be computed once.
quiz.why: SQLite 3.35+, PostgreSQL 12+.

sql28.title: 28. CTE: name each step of the query

sql29.summary: Write a recursive CTE to generate number sequences, continuous date series and traverse multi-level category trees.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: A daily revenue report **misses** days with no orders, so the chart has gaps. A menu category tree has several levels (Drinks → Coffee → Phin coffee). Both need a query that **calls itself**: a recursive CTE.

slides.title: Recursion in the flow diagram
slides.body: The **Recursive** branch: an anchor part (the starting point) plus a recursive part (builds the next rows from the rows just produced) until nothing more is generated.

slides.title: Fixed point
slides.body:
A recursive CTE computes a **fixed point**: it repeats the recursive part over the newest rows until a pass produces no new rows. The idea comes from Datalog, in deductive database research in the years 1980.

> Abiteboul, S., Hull, R. and Vianu, V. (1995) *Foundations of Databases*. Addison-Wesley, ch. 12.

slides.title: Two common patterns
slides.body:
1. **Generate a sequence**: numbers 1→n, first day of the month → last day of the month.
2. **Traverse a tree**: from the root down to the children (categories, org charts, nested comments).

slides.title: Sequence 1 → 10
slides.body: Anchor `SELECT 1`; recursive `n + 1` when `n < 10`. **Always** include a stop condition.

slides.title: Full calendar
slides.body: Every date 10, including days with no orders.

slides.title: Revenue with no gaps
slides.body: LEFT JOIN the calendar with the order count; empty days show 0. (The original sample data only covers the first 3 days.)

slides.title: Traverse the category tree
slides.body: From the root (`parent_id IS NULL`), each step goes down one level; `depth` counts the level, `path` builds the path.

slides.title: All subcategories of Drinks
slides.body: Change the anchor to the starting node.

slides.title: Exercise 1: multiplication table 7
slides.body: Generate 10 rows `n, 7 * n` with n from 1 to 10.

slides.title: Exercise 2: days with no orders
slides.body: For the original sample data, list the days **from 01/10 to 07/10** on which the shop has **no orders**.

hints: Build a full calendar with a recursive CTE.
Filter days with NOT IN the list of days that have orders.

slides.title: Exercise 3: tree depth
slides.body: Show the `name` and `depth` (root = 0) of every category.

hints: Recursive: JOIN cats joined to the tree by parent_id.

quiz.q: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
o: The anchor and recursive member joined with UNION ALL
quiz.why: The anchor runs once; the recursive member repeats.

quiz.q: A recursive CTE with no stop condition can run forever.
quiz.why: Always have a WHERE stop or a LIMIT.

quiz.q: How many rows are there?
Why does a report need a full calendar?
o: Days with no orders still appear, with the value 0
quiz.why: No gaps on the time axis.

quiz.q: Required keyword.
quiz.why: WITH RECURSIVE.

sql29.title: 29. Recursive CTE: category tree and date series

sql30.summary: Calculations over a "window" of rows without collapsing them: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, PARTITION BY and the top-N per group problem.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: GROUP BY collapses rows and **loses** detail. A window function computes over a group of rows but **keeps** each row: ranking dishes within each category, the order number of each customer's purchase. The "top 2 per category" problem, a classic interview question, takes only a few lines.

slides.title: Sliding window
slides.body: Each row sees a **frame** of related rows. This step uses the whole group as the frame (PARTITION); step 32 narrows the frame to a few rows around each row.

slides.title: Window functions in the standard
slides.body:
Window functions entered the standard SQL:2003 (originating in Oracle and IBM's OLAP proposals in 1999). SQLite has supported them since 3.25 (2018). The optimizer needs only **one sort** by PARTITION plus ORDER BY to compute all the columns, much faster than a correlated subquery.

> Leis, V. et al. (2015) 'Efficient processing of window functions in analytical SQL queries', *Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment*, 8(10), pp. 1058–1069.

slides.title: Three ways to number ties
slides.body:
Three drinks each sold 20 cups:

| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| ROW_NUMBER | 1, 2, 3, 4 (always distinct) |
| RANK | 1, 1, 1, 4 (skips) |
| DENSE_RANK | 1, 1, 1, 2 (no gaps) |

slides.title: OVER (ORDER BY …)
slides.body: Rank drinks by cups sold in month 10.

slides.title: PARTITION BY: rank within each group
slides.body: Each drink category renumbers from 1.

slides.title: Top-N per group
slides.body: Don't filter a window function directly in WHERE (it is computed **after** WHERE) → wrap it in CTE and then filter.

slides.title: Customer's order sequence number
slides.body: Number each customer's orders by time: the foundation for cohort analysis (step 38).

slides.title: Aggregate functions as window functions
slides.body: `SUM(…) OVER (PARTITION BY …)` puts the group's total beside each row — computing **shares**.

slides.title: Exercise 1: each customer's first order
slides.body: Show the `customer_id` and `id` **first** orders of each customer (excluding walk-ins).

hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at)
Wrap CTE and then filter rn = 1.

slides.title: Exercise 2: dense rank
slides.body: Show the `name, price` and `DENSE_RANK` by **descending** price (name it `hang`).

quiz.q: How is a window function different from GROUP BY?
quiz.why: Computes over a group without collapsing rows.

quiz.q: Score 20, 20, 15: what is RANK for the row 15?
quiz.why: RANK skips: 1, 1, 3.

quiz.q: Same data, what does DENSE_RANK give the row 15?
quiz.why: No gaps: 1, 1, 2.

quiz.q: Renumber from 1 within each category.
quiz.why: PARTITION BY divides into groups.

quiz.q: Can you write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) = 1 directly?
quiz.why: Window functions are computed after WHERE — wrap CTE and then filter.

sql30.title: 30. Window functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK

sql31.summary: Look at the row before or after with LAG and LEAD: growth versus yesterday, the gap between two purchases, FIRST_VALUE and NTILE.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Question number 5 from the shop owner in step 1: **"Is this month up or down compared with last month?"** To compare a row with the row **before** it you need LAG; with the row **after** it, LEAD.

slides.title: LAG looks back
slides.body: The frame of LAG(x, 1) is exactly **one** row right before the current row (ordered by ORDER BY in OVER).

slides.title: Time-series analysis with SQL
slides.body:
Day-over-day growth, gaps between events, anomaly detection — previously you had to pull the data into Excel or Python. LAG/LEAD (SQL:2003) let you do it inside the database, so the data never leaves the server.

> Winand, M. (2025) *Modern SQL: LAG and LEAD*. Available at: https://modern-sql.com/

slides.title: Three questions over time
slides.body:
1. Today's revenue compared with yesterday: +/− how many %?
2. After how many days does each customer come back?
3. Which customer falls in the highest 25% spending group?

slides.title: LAG: compared with yesterday
slides.body: The first day has no yesterday → NULL. `nullif` avoids dividing by 0.

slides.title: WINDOW: naming a window
slides.body: Writing `OVER (ORDER BY ngay)` three times is long. The `WINDOW w AS (…)` clause names it once.

slides.title: Gap between two purchases
slides.body: LAG per customer (PARTITION), then subtract the two timestamps using julianday.

slides.title: FIRST_VALUE and NTILE
slides.body: `FIRST_VALUE` takes the first value of the frame (the customer's first order). `NTILE(4)` splits into 4 equal groups. Group 1 is the 25% highest spenders.

slides.title: Exercise 1: difference in number of orders
slides.body: CTE `d(ngay, so_don)` counts orders per day (month 10). Show `ngay, so_don` and `so_don - LAG(so_don)` named `chenh`.

hints: The first day's difference is NULL — correct.

slides.title: Exercise 2: next order
slides.body: For customer 2: show `id`, `ordered_at` and the **time of the next order** (`LEAD`), named `don_sau`.

quiz.q: What does LAG(x) return?
quiz.why: LEAD is the following row.

quiz.q: LAG of the first row is NULL (if no default value is given).
quiz.why: LAG(x, 1, default) to replace NULL.

quiz.q: Name a window for reuse.
quiz.why: WINDOW clause.

quiz.q: What is NTILE(4) used for?
quiz.why: Quantiles.

quiz.q: What is needed to compute the number of days between each customer's two consecutive purchases?
quiz.why: LAG within each customer.

sql31.title: 31. LAG, LEAD and time comparisons

sql32.summary: Control window frames with ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN: running totals, a 7-day moving average, and build a complete revenue dashboard.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: Daily revenue rises and falls erratically. The shop owner needs the **trend**: the total since the start of the month (running total) and the average of the last 7 days (moving). Both are window functions with a custom **frame**.

slides.title: Window frame
slides.body: `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: the current row and 2 rows before it. Changing the number changes the frame width.

slides.title: Moving average
slides.body:
A moving average smooths short-term noise to reveal the trend, a basic technique in time-series analysis. Choose 7 days because retail has a clear **weekly cycle**: averaging over 7 days removes the weekend effect.

> Hyndman, R.J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021) *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*. 3rd edn. OTexts, ch. 3. Available at: https://otexts.com/fpp3/ (CC BY-NC-ND — citation only).

slides.title: Revenue dashboard
slides.body: One row per day: revenue, month-to-date running total, 7-day average, rank within the month, % change vs yesterday. One SQL statement — no Excel.

slides.title: Running total
slides.body: By default, `SUM … OVER (ORDER BY ngay)` sets the frame to **from the start up to the current row**.

slides.title: 7-day moving average
slides.body: Explicit frame: 6 rows before + the current row.

slides.title: ROWS or RANGE
slides.body:
- **ROWS**: counts by physical **row number**.
- **RANGE**: by the **value** of ORDER BY. Tied rows are counted together.

The default when ORDER BY is used is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: two days with the same value get the same running total. To count each row individually, state `ROWS` explicitly.

slides.title: Complete dashboard
slides.body: Combine everything from stage 6 into one query.

slides.title: Exercise 1: running total of orders
slides.body: CTE `d(ngay, so_don)`; show `ngay, so_don` and the **running total of orders** `luy_ke`.

hints: Each day is unique, so RANGE and ROWS give the same result.

slides.title: Exercise 2: 3-day average
slides.body: Using the same CTE `d`, show `ngay` and the average number of orders over **3 days** (2 days before + today), rounded to 1 decimal places, named `tb3`.

hints: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

slides.title: Stage 6 summary
slides.body: CTE, CTE recursive, ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD, NTILE, running totals, moving averages, ROWS/RANGE — the analysis toolkit of every data analyst. Stage 7: make them **fast** on millions of rows.

quiz.q: What is the default frame when ORDER BY is in OVER?
o: From the start to the current row (RANGE)
quiz.why: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.

quiz.q: 7-day average.
quiz.why: 6 days before + today = 7.

quiz.q: x = 1, 2, 2, 3. What is SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY x) on the first 2 row?
quiz.why: RANGE groups the two 2 values together at once: 1 + 2 + 2.

quiz.q: ROWS counts by row number, RANGE by the value of ORDER BY.
quiz.why: They differ when there are tied values.

quiz.q: Why does a 7-day moving average suit a coffee shop?
o: It removes the weekly cycle (busy weekends)
quiz.why: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021).

sql32.title: 32. Running totals, moving averages and window frames

sql33.summary: Understand how the B-tree index works, create indexes, measure the difference between a full table scan and an index lookup, and the cost you pay on writes.

slides.title: Stage 7: fast on millions of rows
slides.body:
The Hạt shop now has 50.000 orders (the `big_orders` table in the SQL cell). A query that is correct but **slow** is a wrong query in the user's eyes.

Stage 7: B-tree → EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN → covering/partial/expression indexes → JSON → full-text search.

slides.title: Mind map: stage 7
slides.body: Four branches cover **indexes and query plans**; two cover **special data types** (JSON, text) that need their own indexes.

slides.title: Tree B-tree
slides.body: An index is a **sorted** tree. Looking up a value walks from the root down to a leaf: each step discards half (or more), so it takes log n steps instead of reading n rows. The library card cabinet in step 1 is a wooden index.

slides.title: Bayer and McCreight (1972)
slides.body:
B-tree was invented at Boeing for disk storage: each node fits one disk page, and the tree is shallow so few reads are needed. Almost every relational DBMS — SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL — uses B-tree (or a B+tree variant) as its default index.

> Bayer, R. and McCreight, E. (1972) 'Organization and maintenance of large ordered indexes', *Acta Informatica*, 1(3), pp. 173–189.

slides.title: The most common question
slides.body: The app shows a **customer's order history** every time they open it: `WHERE customer_id = ?`. This query runs thousands of times a day, so it deserves an index.

slides.title: Full table scan
slides.body: Without an index: `SCAN big_orders` — reads all 50.000 rows.

slides.title: CREATE INDEX
slides.body: With an index: `SEARCH … USING INDEX` — jumps straight to about 10 rows needed.

slides.title: Multi-column index
slides.body: Column order matters, like a phone book sorted by (last name, first name): searching by the **first column** or **first + second column** can use the index; searching by the second column alone cannot.

slides.title: The cost of an index
slides.body: Every index is a tree that must be **updated on every write**, and it takes up space. Don't index every column, only the queries that really run often. See the indexes that currently exist:

slides.title: Exercise: index for total amount
slides.body: Create the index `idx_big_total` on `big_orders(total)`, then list `name` the indexes on the `big_orders` table.

quiz.q: How many steps does a lookup in the B-tree index take with n rows?
quiz.why: A balanced tree; each step eliminates most of the rows.

quiz.q: Adding an index makes INSERT/UPDATE slightly slower.
quiz.why: Every index must be updated on each write.

quiz.q: Which WHERE can the index (branch_id, ordered_at) serve?
quiz.why: It must use the leading column (the leftmost prefix).

quiz.q: Create the index.
quiz.why: CREATE INDEX.

quiz.q: Who invented B-tree?
quiz.why: Boeing, 1972.

sql33.title: 33. B-tree index: why it's fast to search

sql34.summary: Read query plans, recognize patterns that defeat an index (functions on a column, LIKE '%…', OR, type casts), and rewrite them to be "sargable".

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: An index is not always **used**. A query written as `WHERE date(ordered_at) = …` leaves the index on `ordered_at` useless. This step teaches reading `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` and fixing the patterns that "kill the index".

slides.title: EXPLAIN in the diagram
slides.body: The **EXPLAIN** branch: ask the DBMS "how do you plan to run this query?" before actually running it.

slides.title: Cost-based optimizer
slides.body:
Selinger et al. (1979) built the cost-based optimizer for System R: enumerate the ways to run a query, estimate the cost of each using statistics, and pick the cheapest. Every modern DBMS still follows this framework. `ANALYZE` collects the statistics for the optimizer.

> Selinger, P.G. et al. (1979) 'Access path selection in a relational database management system', *Proceedings of ACM SIGMOD 1979*, pp. 23–34.

slides.title: Sargable
slides.body: A condition is **sargable** (Search ARGument ABLE) when the column stands **bare** on one side: `cột <toán tử> hằng`. Wrapping the column in a function, arithmetic, or a cast loses the ability to use the index.

slides.title: Function on a column defeats the index
slides.body: There is an index on `ordered_at`, but `date(ordered_at)` → it still **SCANs**: SQLite reads through all 50.000 entries of the index (a bit cheaper than reading the table, but it does not jump straight to the date needed). Compare with the next slide: **SEARCH**.

slides.title: Rewrite as a range
slides.body: Same meaning; bare column → SEARCH USING INDEX.

slides.title: Arithmetic on a column
slides.body: `total / 1000 > 150` → SCAN. Move the arithmetic to the constant side: `total > 150000`.

slides.title: LIKE '%…' and LIKE '…%'
slides.body: A pattern starting with `%` cannot use B-tree. A prefix pattern `'giao%'` can (SQLite needs an index on `COLLATE NOCASE` or `case_sensitive_like` enabled).

slides.title: ANALYZE and reading the JOIN plan
slides.body: `ANALYZE` updates the statistics; the JOIN plan shows which tables are scanned outright and which use an index lookup inside.

slides.title: Exercise: rewrite to be sargable
slides.body: Count orders where `total` is **100.000 or more**, written so an index can be used (`idx_total` is already created). The result is one number.

hints: Remove the division on the column.

quiz.q: Which condition is sargable?
quiz.why: Bare column on one side.

quiz.q: LIKE '%rush' can use the B-tree index.
quiz.why: A pattern starting with % must scan.

quiz.q: Check the execution plan.
quiz.why: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SQLite), EXPLAIN (PostgreSQL).

quiz.q: What is ANALYZE used for?
quiz.why: Selinger (1979): cost-based optimization.

quiz.q: Match each plan to its meaning.
quiz.why: Read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.

sql34.title: 34. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN and query optimization

sql35.summary: Three advanced index types: covering indexes (no table read needed), partial indexes (only the rows needed), expression indexes (for columns wrapped in a function).

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: An index often finds the **location** of a row, but then the table must still be read. The three techniques below cut that work, or make the index much smaller.

slides.title: The three index branches
slides.body: The **Covering** and **Partial** branches of the 7 diagram, plus the **expression** index to rescue the conditions with functions from step 34.

slides.title: Covering index
slides.body:
Winand calls an index that contains every column the query needs an **index-only scan**: the DBMS answers directly from the index tree without touching the table — often dozens of times faster with wide tables.

> Winand, M. (2012) *SQL Performance Explained*, ch. 5 'Clustering Data'. Available at: https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering/index-only-scan-covering-index

slides.title: Three queries to optimize
slides.body:
1. Total amount per branch within a date range → **covering**.
2. Find only the "rush" orders (1% of the table) → **partial**.
3. Search by `date(ordered_at)` without wanting to change the application code → **expression**.

slides.title: Covering index
slides.body: Index containing `branch_id, ordered_at, total` → the plan shows `USING COVERING INDEX`.

slides.title: Partial index
slides.body: `WHERE` in CREATE INDEX: index only about 500 'rush' rows instead of 50.000.

slides.title: Expression index
slides.body: Index the **expression itself** `date(ordered_at)` — the query that is "not sargable" in step 34 can now use the index.

slides.title: UNIQUE index
slides.body: An index is also a **constraint**: a UNIQUE INDEX blocks duplicates. Example: each customer has only one 'open' order — a **partial** unique index.

slides.title: Exercise: index for large orders
slides.body: Create a **partial** index `idx_big` on `big_orders(ordered_at)` for only `total >= 190000` orders, then count such orders.

quiz.q: What is a covering index?
o: An index on every table column
An index that contains every column the query needs
quiz.why: No need to read the table.

quiz.q: A partial index is smaller than a full-table index.
quiz.why: Contains only rows satisfying WHERE.

quiz.q: Rescue WHERE date(ordered_at) = … without changing the query?
quiz.why: The expression matches the index exactly.

quiz.q: Block duplicates with an index.
quiz.why: Partial unique index.

quiz.q: What does the plan line USING COVERING INDEX mean?
o: Answer from the index alone, without reading the table
quiz.why: Index-only scan.

sql35.title: 35. Covering index, partial index, expression index

sql36.summary: Store and query semi-structured data with JSON: extract fields with ->>, expand arrays with json_each, build JSON from a table, and know when NOT to use JSON.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: The Hạt app sends events with different shapes (orders, reviews, errors). Creating a table for each type is cumbersome; storing **JSON** is flexible, and modern SQL can query JSON directly.

slides.title: JSON in the diagram
slides.body: The **JSON** branch: the `->` operator (gets child JSON), `->>` (gets the SQL value), and the `json_each` function (expands an array into rows).

slides.title: JSON in the SQL standard:2016
slides.body:
SQL:2016 standardizes the JSON functions (JSON_VALUE, JSON_TABLE…). PostgreSQL has a binary `jsonb` type with a GIN index; SQLite stores JSON as text and has the operators `->` / `->>`, like PostgreSQL from the 3.38 version.

> ISO/IEC (2016) *ISO/IEC TR 19075-6:2017 SQL support for JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)*.

slides.title: When to use JSON
slides.body:
- **Yes**: auxiliary data, changing shape, rarely filtered (device info, configuration).
- **No**: foreign keys, money, columns that are often filtered or JOIN. You need real columns for constraints and indexes.

slides.title: ->> gets the value
slides.body: `payload ->> '$.device.os'` follows the JSON path.

slides.title: Filter and group by the JSON field
slides.body: Average rating by operating system.

slides.title: json_each: expand array
slides.body: Each element of `items` becomes a row, turning JSON into a table so JOIN.

slides.title: Create JSON from a table
slides.body: `json_object` and `json_group_array` build JSON that feeds directly into API.

slides.title: Index on the JSON field
slides.body: An expression index (step 35) can be applied to JSON.

slides.title: Exercise 1: 5-star reviews
slides.body: Show the `text` of reviews that have `stars = 5`.

slides.title: Exercise 2: total cups from events
slides.body: Use `json_each` to compute the **total number of cups** across all `order` events.

quiz.q: How do -> and ->> differ?
o: -> returns JSON, ->> returns the SQL value
quiz.why: Same as PostgreSQL.

quiz.q: Expand the JSON array into rows.
quiz.why: The json_each table function.

quiz.q: Should foreign keys and money be stored in JSON for flexibility?
quiz.why: Real columns are needed for constraints and indexes.

quiz.q: Block JSON from being corrupted on write?
quiz.why: A CHECK constraint.

quiz.q: Speed up filtering by the JSON field?
quiz.why: An expression index.

sql37.summary: Full-text search with the FTS virtual table: MATCH, prefix search, phrases, AND/OR/NOT, removing Vietnamese diacritics, ranking, and the difference between FTS4 and FTS5.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: The conclusion of step 8: `LIKE '%cà phê%'` is slow on large tables and does not understand unaccented Vietnamese. **Full-text search** indexes each **word**: typing "ca phe" still returns "Cà phê", instantly.

slides.title: FTS in the diagram
slides.body: The **FTS** branch: an inverted index. Each word points to the list of documents containing it, like a book's back-of-the-book index.

slides.title: Inverted index
slides.body:
Every search engine, from Google to Elasticsearch, is built on an **inverted index**. Result ranking commonly uses BM25, the probabilistic model by Robertson et al. SQLite FTS5 has the `bm25()` function built in.

> Manning, C.D., Raghavan, P. and Schütze, H. (2008) *Introduction to Information Retrieval*. Cambridge University Press, ch. 1 & 11.

slides.title: Menu search box, the full version
slides.body: Type "ca phe lanh" → Cold brew ("cà phê ủ lạnh"). Type "tra" → every item containing the word trà. Type "sua -dac" → items with sữa but not sữa đặc.

slides.title: The FTS virtual table and MATCH
slides.body: `tokenize=unicode61 "remove_diacritics=2"` strips Vietnamese diacritics when indexing and when searching.

slides.title: Prefix search
slides.body: `tra*` matches "trà" and "trái". Useful when the user is still typing.

slides.title: Phrases and logic operators
slides.body: Double quotes = exact phrase in order. `OR`, and the `-` sign (NOT, FTS4 standard form) excludes.

slides.title: Search within one column and snippets
slides.body: `cột:từ` restricts to a column; `snippet()` returns a snippet with the keyword highlighted for display.

slides.title: How is FTS5 different?
slides.body:
The full SQLite build (Node, Python, Android) has **FTS5**, newer than FTS4:

~~~sql
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE menu_fts USING fts5(name, description, tokenize = 'unicode61 remove_diacritics 2');
SELECT name, bm25(menu_fts) AS diem FROM menu_fts WHERE menu_fts MATCH 'ca phe' ORDER BY diem;
~~~

- Has built-in `bm25()` ranking, `highlight()`.
- Clear `NOT` syntax, with prefixes via a separate index (`prefix='2 3'`).

PostgreSQL uses `tsvector` + a GIN index for the same purpose.

slides.title: Exercise 1: items with milk
slides.body: Find the names of items containing the word "sữa" (type without diacritics).

hints: MATCH 'sua' — FTS has already stripped the diacritics.
SELECT name FROM menu_fts WHERE menu_fts MATCH …

slides.title: Exercise 2: search only the name
slides.body: Find items whose name starts with "ca" **in the name column**.

slides.title: Stage 7 summary
slides.body: You now know why queries are fast or slow: B-tree, query plans, sargable conditions, covering, partial and expression indexes, JSON with indexes, full-text search. Stage 8: the **capstone project**, a real report for the Hạt shop.

quiz.q: How is FTS different from LIKE '%x%'?
o: Uses a word-based inverted index, is fast, and can ignore diacritics
Only matches the start of a string
quiz.why: Inverted index.

quiz.q: Prefix search for 'tra'.
quiz.why: The * after a word.

quiz.q: remove_diacritics lets 'ca phe' find 'cà phê'.
quiz.why: Strip diacritics when indexing and when searching.

quiz.q: Which ranking function is built into FTS5?
quiz.why: Robertson et al. — BM25.

quiz.q: What does PostgreSQL use for full-text search?
quiz.why: The equivalent of FTS in SQLite.

sql38.summary: Combine every technique from the course into one real analysis: group customers by the week of their first purchase, measure the weekly return rate, and segment with RFM.

slides.title: Stage 8: graduation
slides.body: The last three steps teach no new syntax. They **combine** everything: CTE, window functions, JOIN, CASE, dates and times. This step asks the most important question for any shop: **do customers come back?**

slides.title: Mind map: the shop report Hạt
slides.body: Six reports make up the capstone project. This step builds **Cohort** and **Customers (RFM)**; step 40 builds all six.

slides.title: Cohort and RFM analysis
slides.body:
**Cohort** groups customers by their start time (the week of their first purchase), then tracks each group's behavior over time. This avoids mixing new and returning customers together.

**RFM** (Recency – Frequency – Monetary) segments customers by whether they bought recently, how often they buy, and how much they spend.

> Fader, P.S., Hardie, B.G.S. and Lee, K.L. (2005) 'RFM and CLV: using iso-value curves for customer base analysis', *Journal of Marketing Research*, 42(4), pp. 415–430.

slides.title: Cohort steps
slides.body:
1. `first`: each customer's first purchase week (MIN).
2. `activity`: how many weeks after the first week each order falls.
3. Count distinct customers by (cohort, week k).
4. Divide by cohort size → return rate.

slides.title: Steps 1–2: first week and week k
slides.body: Each customer's first purchase, then how many **weeks** after that first purchase each order falls (divide the number of days by 7 and keep the integer part).

slides.title: Cohort table
slides.body: Cohort = the week within the month of the first purchase (`%W` = number of weeks in the year). Each cell: the number of customers in that cohort who still buy in week k.

slides.title: RFM
slides.body: Each customer gets three numbers, then NTILE(3) splits them into groups 1 (best) → 3.

slides.title: Exercise: return rate
slides.body: Calculate the **percentage of customers** (excluding walk-ins) who have **2 or more orders** in the month, rounded to 1 decimal places.

hints: SUM(n >= 2) counts the customers who meet the condition (TRUE = 1).

quiz.q: In customer analysis, what is a cohort?
o: A group of customers who started at the same time
quiz.why: Track each group over time.

quiz.q: Match the RFM letters.
quiz.why: Fader et al. (2005).

quiz.q: Join on same-named columns.
quiz.why: USING (column) instead of ON a.c = b.c.

quiz.q: SUM(n >= 2) counts the rows where n is 2 or more in SQLite.
quiz.why: Comparison returns 1 or 0.

sql39.summary: Carry the knowledge over to PostgreSQL and MySQL: a comparison of data types, auto-increment, date-time, strings, UPSERT, JSON, and search, plus how to choose a DBMS.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body: About 90% of what you learned is **identical** in every DBMS: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, CTE, and window functions. The remaining 10% is "dialect". This step is a lookup table so you won't be lost moving to PostgreSQL (Supabase, Neon) or MySQL.

slides.title: Full course map
slides.body: The eight branches you've worked through are all **SQL standard**. The main differences lie in the Design branch (data types) and Performance (DBMS-specific indexes).

slides.title: Standards compliance
slides.body:
No DBMS fully complies with the SQL standard. PostgreSQL is usually considered the closest to standard among open-source systems; MySQL has many proprietary extensions; SQLite is deliberately minimal but increasingly complete (window functions 2018, RETURNING 2021, STRICT 2021).

> Winand, M. (2025) *Modern SQL — feature comparison*. Available at: https://modern-sql.com/

slides.title: Data types
slides.body:
| Concept | SQLite | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integer | INTEGER | integer / bigint | INT / BIGINT |
| Exact money | INTEGER (whole đồng) | numeric(12,0) | DECIMAL(12,0) |
| Text | TEXT | text / varchar | VARCHAR(n) / TEXT |
| Date-time | TEXT ISO 8601 | timestamptz | DATETIME |
| Boolean | 0/1 | boolean | TINYINT(1) |
| JSON | TEXT + json_* | jsonb | JSON |

slides.title: Auto-increment and date-time
slides.body:
| Task | SQLite | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auto-increment id | INTEGER PRIMARY KEY | GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY | AUTO_INCREMENT |
| Now | datetime('now') | now() | NOW() |
| Get date | date(t) | t::date | DATE(t) |
| Add 7 days | date(t, '+7 days') | t + interval '7 days' | t + INTERVAL 7 DAY |
| Hour | strftime('%H', t) | extract(hour from t) | HOUR(t) |

slides.title: Strings, UPSERT, search
slides.body:
| Task | SQLite | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concatenate | a \|\| b | a \|\| b | CONCAT(a, b) |
| Aggregate into a string | group_concat | string_agg | GROUP_CONCAT |
| UPSERT | ON CONFLICT | ON CONFLICT | ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE |
| Get the row just written | RETURNING | RETURNING | (none — LAST_INSERT_ID()) |
| Case-insensitive | LIKE (ASCII) | ILIKE | default, per collation |
| Full-text | FTS5 | tsvector + GIN | FULLTEXT |
| Parameters | ? | $1, $2 | ? |

slides.title: Choosing a DBMS
slides.body:
- **SQLite**: mobile apps, single-user tools, prototypes, data bundled with an app.
- **PostgreSQL**: the default choice for multi-user web; JSON, full-text search, strong extensibility.
- **MySQL/MariaDB**: common shared hosting and the PHP/WordPress ecosystem (the Coding course uses MySQL).

Free tiers to practice on: Supabase, Neon (PostgreSQL).

slides.title: Practice: translate a query
slides.body:
Translate this SQLite query into PostgreSQL (write it on paper or in a `hat/dialects.md` file):

~~~sql
SELECT strftime('%H', ordered_at) AS gio, group_concat(id, ',') AS don
FROM orders
WHERE ordered_at >= date('now', '-7 days')
GROUP BY gio;
~~~

Suggested answer: `extract(hour from ordered_at)`, `string_agg(id::text, ',')`, `now() - interval '7 days'`.

quiz.q: Match the task to PostgreSQL syntax.
quiz.why: PostgreSQL dialect.

quiz.q: How do you write UPSERT in MySQL?
quiz.why: MySQL has no ON CONFLICT.

quiz.q: CTE and the window functions you learned in SQLite work almost unchanged on PostgreSQL.
quiz.why: Both are SQL standard.

quiz.q: Which date-time type with time zone is recommended in PostgreSQL?
quiz.why: Stored in UTC, displayed in the session time zone.

sql40.summary: Capstone project: write 10 real report queries for the Hạt shop on month 10's data (revenue, dishes, customers, peak hours, trends), each auto-graded.

slides.title: Capstone project
slides.body:
The owner of Hạt assigns you **10 questions**. Each question is an auto-graded SQL cell on month 10's data (12 customers, 120 orders). There are no sample answers, only hints when you get one wrong.

General convention: **revenue** = `SUM(qty * price)`; walk-in orders have `customer_id` NULL.

slides.title: Six report areas
slides.body: Ten questions cover six areas: revenue, dishes, customers, cohorts, peak hours, and trends.

slides.title: Reports must be traceable
slides.body:
The principle of data auditing: every figure in a report must be **traceable** back to the raw data by a clear query. So write CTE with clear names and a comment `--` for each step.

> Kimball, R. and Ross, M. (2013) *The Data Warehouse Toolkit*. 3rd edn. Indianapolis: Wiley, ch. 1.

slides.title: 1. Monthly revenue
slides.body: Total revenue for the whole month 10 (one number).

slides.title: 2. Revenue by day
slides.body: `ngay` and revenue per day, sorted by day in ascending order.

slides.title: 3. Top 3 menu items by revenue
slides.body: Name and revenue of the **3 menu items** with the highest revenue, highest first.

hints: GROUP BY m.id, ORDER BY revenue DESC.

slides.title: 4. Average order value
slides.body: Average value **per order**, rounded to the nearest đồng.

slides.title: 5. Peak hours
slides.body: The hour (`strftime('%H', …)`) with **the most orders** and the number of orders in that hour.

slides.title: 6. Customers who spend the most
slides.body: Name and total spend of the **2 customers** who spend the most.

slides.title: 7. Share of revenue by category
slides.body: Each `category` and its **% of revenue** out of the total, rounded to 1 decimal places.

hints: Window function on the aggregated result: SUM(SUM(…)) OVER ().

slides.title: 8. Best-selling item per category
slides.body: One row per `category`: the item name with **the most cups** sold in that category.

hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY SUM(qty) DESC)
Wrap CTE and then filter rn = 1.

slides.title: 9. Week-over-week growth
slides.body: Each week (`strftime('%W', …)`) and revenue, with **the change from the previous week** (column name `chenh`).

slides.title: 10. 7-day moving average
slides.body: Each `ngay` and the average revenue over the **7 most recent days** (including that day), rounded to the nearest đồng.

hints: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

slides.body:
You have gone from a handwritten notebook to reports built with CTE, window functions, indexes and full-text search, exactly the path a Data Analyst or Backend Developer needs.

**Next steps:**
- Practice on a free PostgreSQL (Supabase, Neon).
- Read *Use The Index, Luke* (Winand) to go deeper into performance.
- Unlock **Web Programming** to connect SQL to a real application.

Education Hugo will stay with you through every lesson ahead.
